If you are working toward American AAdvantage elite status this qualification year, you may be looking for more ways to earn Loyalty Points to secure your desired status. Here's what you need to know about AAdvantage elite status requirements and five ways to close your Loyalty Point gap before the end of February.

The status qualification year for American AAdvantage elite status runs from March 1 to the end of February. You need the following number of Loyalty Points to qualify for each status tier:

Your Loyalty Points reset to zero each year on March 1. However, once you earn AAdvantage elite status, you'll keep it through March 31 of the year following the end of your qualification year.

Related: American AAdvantage miles vs. Loyalty Points: What's the difference?

Loyalty Points are the sole metric for AAdvantage elite status. As a reminder, you generally earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile you earn, including miles earned through flights, credit card spending and select partners.

However, some AAdvantage miles — including those earned through credit card welcome offers and certain promotional bonuses — don't earn Loyalty Points.

Related: The best American Airlines Loyalty Point Rewards at every milestone

Here are five straightforward ways to earn more Loyalty Points before the current elite qualification year ends on Feb. 28.

You can earn Loyalty Points on eligible flights with American Airlines and its partners. Flights marketed by American and select partners, including British Airways and Iberia, earn 5 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on eligible fares, plus elite status bonuses. Other partners, including Alaska Airlines, Finnair and Japan Airlines, award Loyalty Points based on fare class and distance flown.

Basic economy tickets usually don't earn Loyalty Points.

If you have the (see rates and fees), you can also earn 5,000 bonus Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to three times per qualification year.

Related: How to earn American Airlines AAdvantage miles

You can earn Loyalty Points by shopping through the AAdvantage eShopping portal or using eligible SimplyMiles offers with an enrolled Mastercard. However, Loyalty Points generally won't post until the qualifying transaction is completed and processed, which may be long after you purchase back-ordered items and hotel stays.

Related: Earn points, miles or cash back: How to maximize online shopping portals for your purchases

When you book your stay through AAdvantage Hotels, you can earn up to 15,000 Loyalty Points per reservation once you complete your stay. However, keep in mind that you usually won't get hotel elite status earning or benefits when you book through AAdvantage Hotels.

Related: How I earned 29,000 Loyalty Points and 23,000 AAdvantage miles on a single $800 hotel stay

You can earn Loyalty Points at participating AAdvantage Dining restaurants. Just be sure to register your favorite dining rewards cards in the AAdvantage Dining program — which will unregister them from most other dining rewards programs — and then use an enrolled card to pay at participating restaurants.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

You can also earn Loyalty Points when you use AAdvantage credit cards for purchases. Specifically, you'll generally earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent on eligible purchases with an AAdvantage credit card, regardless of whether the card earns bonus miles in certain spending categories. Purchases made through Feb. 28, 2027, will earn Loyalty Points that count toward the status qualification year ending on Feb. 28, 2027, even if your statement closes in March.

The (see rates and fees) also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds — 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points — for up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per qualification year. These thresholds include Loyalty Points earned through all eligible methods, not just card spending.

Related: Which AAdvantage card is right for you? Here are 3 options you should consider

American AAdvantage has yet to announce whether it will change its elite status tiers or qualification requirements for the next qualification year, which will run from March 1, 2027, to Feb. 29, 2028.

If you're short on Loyalty Points for your desired AAdvantage elite status, you still have time to close the gap before Feb. 28, 2027. Whether you fly, shop, dine, book hotels or spend on an AAdvantage credit card, be sure to understand when your activity will count toward status qualification.

#6176. Military Member Calls Alaska Airlines Employee “Anti-Military” Over Denied Free Upgrade

A military member and social media influencer has taken to Instagram to complain about a recent interaction with an Alaska Airlines employee, where he asked for a free upgrade, and was denied. He’s accusing an employee at the airline of being anti-military. Is that a fair complaint, or is this being blown out of proportion?

A military member posted a 2min35sec video online, outlining his experience with an Alaska Airlines representative at Portland International Airport (PDX), which he claims was his first time encountering an “anti-military” employee at the airline. To summarize his version of events:

You can see the video for yourself below. As you’d expect, this guy’s followers are mostly military related, so the 1,300+ comments on the post are almost entirely in agreement with the person who posted the video.

First let me say that I of course respect and appreciate the service of those who are in the military (even if I fundamentally disagree with the extent to which we get into conflicts that accomplish nothing — that’s the fault of our elected leaders, and not the fault of those who put their lives on the line).

Of course if the Alaska Airlines employee in question was rude, that’s not acceptable, and people expect polite service. Now, I’m a little skeptical of how much of a direct transcript this was, rather than how this guy chose to interpret it. That includes things like him suggesting that the Alaska employee accused him of lying. If that were the case, that’s unacceptable, but again, it’s not clear if that was actually said, or just how he was made to feel.

All that being said, this guy sort of strikes me as being rather entitled. Airlines are extremely generous with active duty military members, as they should be. The airline has a page that outlines military and veteran benefits, and upgrades isn’t among those perks. The airline offers all kinds of other things, ranging from special fares, to lounge access, to priority boarding. But it seems a little greedy to then be like “oh, they do all these things, but they should do more” (since he chooses to reference this page).

But here’s my bigger issue with this guy’s approach. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with asking for an upgrade, but be ready to be shot down. However, I feel like his approach is more one of entitlement than “it can’t hurt to ask.” Why do I say that?

The very example he gives is that for all these times he flies Alaska, either they say “sure, we’ll upgrade you,” or they say “sorry, it’s full, we can’t upgrade you.” In other words, he assumes he’s entitled to the upgrade as long as there are open seats, which just isn’t the policy. If he’s going to be rejected for something he’s not entitled to, he wants to be lied to, rather than told “sorry, that’s not our policy.”

And again, he emphasizes how he has no level of entitlement, but also then argues by pointing out that he has been upgraded for free in the past. It all sounds to me a little like being caught with a liquid that’s too large at the TSA checkpoint, and then trying to argue with them, and say “well last time they let me through.” Well, that’s fine, but that’s not the policy.

So my take here is that airline employees should of course always be professional. I think it’s perfectly fine to say “I’m sorry, that’s not our policy,” which is something this guy seems to take issue with. If the employee did actually accuse him of lying about being upgraded in the past, that’s of course not acceptable. But I’m also not convinced that actually happened.

A military member has accused an Alaska Airlines employee of being anti-military, after being denied a free upgrade to a seat with more legroom. He argues that there’s no harm in asking, but also seems to think that the only acceptable rejection is a claim that the cabin is full.

While Alaska offers lots of perks to military members (as they should), upgrades isn’t among them. Asking once is one thing, but I do find it a bit entitled to essentially believe that you’re entitled to the seats as long as they’re empty, and then to argue if you’re not upgraded.

What do you make of this “anti-military” Alaska employee?

It's always a matter of which uniform deserves greater perks. The guy who plays the flute in the Marine Band? Or the cop who patrols the streets of a high-crime neighborhood? The firefighter going to train for jumping into forest fires? If there is a military preference, there should also be a public safety preference. #6175. Atmos Global Concierge: Alaska Airlines’ New Invitation-Only Elite Status

Alaska Airlines is increasingly becoming like the “big three” US carriers when it comes to its route network, as the airline expands globally, following its takeover of Hawaiian Airlines. Now the airline is doing another thing you’ll find at competitors, which is introducing an invitation-only elite status. Let’s take a look at what we know so far about Atmos Global Concierge, which is the name of this new status.

Some Atmos Rewards members on Reddit are reporting receiving an invitation for the carrier’s new status tier that has no published qualification requirements, and it’s above the Titanium tier. Those who have been awarded the status can keep it through December 31, 2027.

So, what are the perks of Atmos Global Concierge status?

We’ll have to of course wait some time to get firsthand reports of the experience, but as you’d expect, this is a lot more about better “soft” treatment, plus having top priority for everything. There’s nothing particularly remarkable about this status otherwise, but that’s not surprising, since that’s typically not the focus on invitation-only elite status.

It’s anyone’s guess what exactly it takes to get an invitation, as it’s a bit of a mystery, much like with American Concierge Key, Delta 360, and United Global Services. It’s possible that criteria differ based on where you mostly fly out of. It does seem like frequent international travel in business class is something that increases odds of eligibility.

Based on the reports so far, it almost seems like this status is being dangled as a “carrot” for those who have maybe taken a few long haul business class trips, in hopes of keeping them flying on Alaska and Hawaiian.

There’s a reason that airlines offer invitation-only elite status, and it’s kind of brilliant. The idea is to keep people on the “hamster wheel,” and keep them booking high yield tickets on an airline over competitors.

Airlines of course have elite tiers with published requirements, and once you qualify for your planned tier for a year, you might consider branching out and booking another airline. But when there’s invitation-only elite status, you don’t know what you actually need to earn it, so you’re more likely to keep flying with the airline. And if you’re spending other people’s money, you’re also more likely to make sure that ticket is expensive as it should be.

At the end of the day, these kinds of status tiers aren’t really about the exact details of the perks. On some level, they’re intended to stroke the egos of travelers, and that works. People get excited when they get to board a flight first, etc., and this whole concept plays into that.

Alaska Airlines has introduced a new invitation-only elite status, named Atmos Global Concierge. The idea is that this is targeted primarily at those flying a lot internationally, and it offers perks like concierge assistance, upgrade priority, some partner elite perks, and more.

With the way Alaska has grown, it’s not surprising to see the airline also copying the “big three” with a status tier like this.

What do you make of Atmos Global Concierge?

#6174. The Legal Origin Story of Wokeness Is a Map to Defeating Woke 2.0

Students walk between classes on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, Pa., in 2017.

Gail Heriot — a University of San Diego Law School professor who, having spent decades working in civil rights law at a high level, is an exceedingly rare specimen on the right — has brought needed attention to the overlooked story of wokeness’s origins in policy and law. It’s one we need to understand fully if we’re to pursue a solution that actually rolls back the “woke exceptions” to anti-discrimination law that have gutted meritocracy, encouraged bigotry, shut down national conversations, and generally poisoned race relations in our multiethnic republic.

In Why We Walk on Eggshells, a recent release from Encounter Books, Heriot builds a nearly unassailable case that many of these pernicious effects are not “politics downstream from culture,” but rather “culture downstream from law.”

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

#6173. Frontier Airlines’ Unique First Class Now On Sale (No Food, Drinks, Or Recline)

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale, with the product launching systemwide for flights as of March 2027. This is a major development for the Denver-based airline, as the historically ultra low cost carrier tries to move upmarket, and respond to consumer preferences. This is only one of several initiatives we’re seeing, along with the introduction of Starlink Wi-Fi, plus charging ports at select seats. Let’s cover all the details.

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027. For context, Frontier plans to reconfigure its entire fleet to add eight first class seats at the front of the cabin, with two rows of seats in a 2-2 configuration. Specifically, the airline has selected the Geven Comoda seating platform, with seats having up to 37″ of pitch.

Frontier has already started reconfiguring planes with first class cabins, and the idea is that by early March 2027, the entire fleet will have these seats, which is the point at which they’ll be sold as a separate product. So while the seats will already be in service, and some customers will luck out, that’s the formal launch plan.

Obviously this is a fast timeline for retrofitting cabins, but keep in mind most of the cabin will remain unchanged, so it shouldn’t take much time to reconfigure each aircraft. So, what should we expect in terms of the first class product? Here’s how the airline describes it:

First Class seats offer our most spacious seating experience, providing exceptional comfort and additional personal space at the front of the aircraft. These seats are pre-reclined and do not convert into lie-flat beds.

Complimentary food and beverages are not included with the First Class experience. However, a variety of food and beverage options are available for purchase by all passengers.

Frontier’s first class seats will be “pre-reclined” (meaning they won’t recline), and won’t actually offer complimentary snacks and drinks, so it’ll be just like economy in that regard. On the plus side, the seats are expected to feature USB-C charging ports, which will be the first time that the airline offers in-seat power. The carrier is also going from offering no Wi-Fi, to offering Starlink Wi-Fi as of mid-2027, so that’s pretty exciting.

The airline will also be introducing a dedicated extra legroom section in rows three through eight, with seats having up to 34″ of pitch. Not only that, but these seats will also have USB-C charging ports (while the remainder of economy seats won’t offer in-seat power).

With Frontier Airlines first class tickets now on sale, what is pricing like? The airline is increasingly leaning into the concept of bundles, so we’ll see the Basic Fare, Economy Bundle, Premium Bundle, and First Bundle.

The First Bundle includes a carry-on bag and personal item, two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds each, priority boarding, and no change or cancel fees.

Pulling up a random one-way flight from Denver (DEN) to Los Angeles (LAX), I see the Basic Fare starting at $119, the Economy Bundle starting at $142, the Premium Bundle starting at $172, and the First Bundle starting at $244.

Those are some incredibly attractive prices, especially if you intend to check bags. However, the airline emphasizes how it has promotional pricing at launch, so only time will tell how that pricing evolves.

There’s no single right or wrong way to offer a premium product. However, I feel like Frontier might be taking the wrong strategy here. What Frontier is offering is essentially more along the lines of the initial Spirit “Big Front Seat” — you get more space, and nothing else.

This just strikes me as a missed opportunity, because I feel like psychologically, willingness to pay is going to be substantially higher if you just include free alcoholic drinks and at least some sort of food. It’s not like I was expecting them to install ovens and have hot meals (JetBlue’s new first class will only have cold food).

But I feel like if the airline just invested $10 in drinks & snacks they could charge more, and would also expand the potential customer base. Whether logical or not, there are some number of passengers who would be more likely to even consider a product if it actually had a dedicated soft product, rather than just being a more spacious seat. At least that’s my take.

Obviously at the current pricing, this is an incredibly attractive proposition for customers. However, I also feel like the airline probably wants to be able to charge higher fares in the long run.

Frontier Airlines has started to reconfigure planes with first class seats, with tickets now being on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027 (at which point the entire fleet should be reconfigured). While Frontier first class will have first class-style seats (minus the recline), there won’t be any differentiation in terms of the soft product, as food and drinks will still be available for purchase.

I would’ve liked the airline to actually roll out a differentiated soft product, but it sounds like that’s not happening. Then again, between Starlink Wi-Fi and in-seat power, this will be a much more attractive proposition than flying with Frontier in the past.

What do you make of Frontier’s first class concept?

#6172. Diverted Alaska Airlines Passengers Sleep On Red Cross Cots As Carrier Won't Cover Hotels

This article was updated on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, to include further details on Alaska Airlines' other flights from Dallas/Fort Worth. It was originally published on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

Passengers on an Alaska Airlines flight from Dallas to Seattle spent the night sleeping on Red Cross cots inside a regional airport terminal after their aircraft was diverted. Despite apparently promising to cover hotel costs, Alaska Airlines did not provide rooms or meal vouchers for the 127 passengers, leaving local emergency services, the Red Cross and airport staff to intervene.

Flight AS322 diverted to Yakima Air Terminal (YKM) on November 7 after abandoning its approach to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) amid severe weather. However, a faulty fuel indicator then grounded the Boeing 737-900ER overnight. Alaska Airlines reportedly did not provide rooms or vouchers because the initial diversion was weather-related.

AS322, with 127 passengers and eight crew on board, departed Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) at 6:56 PM local time on Saturday, around 50 minutes behind schedule. The Boeing 737-900ER, registered as N277AK, was en route to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) when poor weather forced the crew to abandon its approach.

The flight diverted to Yakima, roughly 100 miles from Seattle, and landed safely at around 9:25 PM. However, while the 737 was being refueled, a faulty fuel indicator was discovered, grounding the plane until engineers coming from Seattle could inspect it. According to NBC Right Now, passengers remained on board for more than two hours after landing and were not allowed to disembark until around 12:15 AM.

They were then informed that the flight would not continue until the following day. According to passenger Michael Pinter, those on the flight were "offered rooms" by an Alaska Airlines rep, who later went home at around midnight. However, Alaska Airlines classified the original diversion as weather-related.

This meant that it considered the disruption outside its control and ultimately did not provide hotel accommodation or meal vouchers, according to the Yakima Herald-Republic. Simple Flying contacted Alaska Airlines for comment, but a representative could not be reached before publication.

With up to 127 passengers needing somewhere to stay, Yakima Air Terminal Director Christopher Hopkins arranged assistance from the American Red Cross. The organization brought in various supplies, including cots, blankets, toiletries, baby formula, and water. Staff from Alaska Airlines' subsidiary Horizon Air also bought Taco Bell for passengers on Saturday night.

Meanwhile, local authorities provided breakfast burritos the following morning. It is reported that around 50 passengers ultimately spent the night in the terminal, sleeping on cots provided by the Red Cross, while the remaining passengers presumably made their own hotel or onward travel arrangements.

Diverted to Yakima due to weather, then grounded overnight by a faulty fuel indicator

Passengers' bags also remained on the aircraft, and they were told that if they left the terminal, there would be no re-entry as TSA facilities were uncrewed. Later that night, at around 4:00 AM, passengers were forced to move out of the secure area. According to Pinter, many ended up sleeping in an under-construction office and meeting space for the remainder of the night.

Members of Alaska Airlines' maintenance team arrived on Sunday morning to inspect the aircraft, which eventually departed Yakima at 2:02 PM as flight AS9230, landing in Seattle around 30 minutes later. Yakima is a regular diversion airport for Seattle-bound flights impacted by poor weather.

Its own scheduled service is limited, with Horizon Air operating two daily flights to Seattle under the Alaska Airlines brand. Yakima has handled notable diversions before, including two Seattle-bound Delta flights with more than 300 passengers in March this year, prompting changes to the airport's readiness program.

From Gander to Shannon, these airports serve as aviation's ultimate safety nets, handling emergency diversions and ETOPS operations across the world

Like most major US airlines, Alaska Airlines determines its hotel and meal assistance based on whether a disruption is within its control. According to its website, the carrier will offer complimentary hotel rooms and ground transportation for overnight disruptions it is responsible for, provided passengers are at least 100 miles from home. It also offers meals for delays of three hours or more.

However, it excludes disruptions caused by weather, air traffic control, passenger illness, and other circumstances deemed outside its control. The situation at Yakima is not so straightforward. While the flight was initially diverted for a reason outside the airline's control, the aircraft was ultimately grounded by a mechanical fault rather than the weather.

The rules determining which disruptions airlines are held responsible for are also set to change next year. Under a new DOT rule, ten causes will be excluded from an airline's control, including unscheduled maintenance that cannot be deferred. As Simple Flying previously explored, this could mean fewer disruptions qualify for hotel accommodation and other assistance.

Seattle is one of three West Coast airports that Alaska Airlines serves from Dala/Fort Worth on a regularly scheduled basis using Boeing 737 narrowbody twinjets from its mainline fleet. According to scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, asn as seen above, its other routes from the Texan airport serve Portland International Airport (PDX) and San Diego International Airport (SAN).

This month, the route to Seattle dwarfs the other two in terms of frequency, with four flights a day typically serving this domestic corridor. Meanwhile, San Diego sees two daily rotations, compared to just one for Portland. With Alaska Airlines being a oneworld member, and DFW being a hub for its alliance partner American Airlines, these flights likely get a lot of connecting traffic as well as point-to-point flyers.

#6171. Lufthansa’s First Airbus A350-1000 Has Arrived: 299.5 Seats, Four Cabins, Munich Routes

In 2023, Lufthansa Group placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000 — the order was initially for 10 frames, before being increased to 15 frames the following year. The Lufthansa Group is undergoing a massive long haul fleet modernization at the moment, with both Airbus and Boeing planes on the way.

Along those lines, the first Lufthansa A350-1000 has just joined the carrier’s fleet (in a dazzling livery no less), so let’s cover all the details, including the routes the plane will fly, how the plane is configured, etc.

Between late 2026 and 2030, Lufthansa is taking delivery of 15 Airbus A350-1000s. This is only one of several aircraft types the airline is acquiring, as it’s also taking delivery of Airbus A350-900s, Boeing 787-9s, and (eventually) Boeing 777-9s.

The first A350-1000 has just been delivered today, with three more planes expected to be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of the year. This first plane even features the special 100th anniversary livery, as Lufthansa has seven of these flying, with one representing each fleet type.

The first plane has the registration code D-AIFA, and is named “Deutschland” (since Lufthansa names all of its planes). This is a special plane for another reason, as it’s also the 700th aircraft that Airbus has delivered to Lufthansa Group. How gorgeous is this plane?!?

Here’s how Heiko Reitz, Lufthansa’s Hub Manager for Munich, describes this:

“We are proud that the Airbus A350-1000—Airbus’s most modern long-haul aircraft—is coming to Munich. The introduction of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization in the history of the Lufthansa Group and a key driver on the path to more sustainability. Our new flagship features 40 percent more Business and Premium Economy seats. To put it simply: The A350-1000 strengthens our premium hub in Munich.”

On a slight tangent, over the summer I saw the 100th anniversary Boeing 747-8 in Frankfurt (FRA), and I must say, I think it might be the most breathtaking plane in commercial service. Is it just me?

We’ve known that the Airbus A350-1000s will get the new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris first class and Allegris business class. So, what can we expect in terms of the configuration? The A350-1000 features 300 seats, spread across four cabins, as follows:

As a point of comparison, the A350-900 (the non-stretched version of the plane) features 267 seats, as follows:

So the stretched version has 11 more business class seats, 11 more premium economy seats, and 11 more economy seats (11 more seats across three cabins, what a funny coincidence). The airline is still maintaining only one row of first class, which is kind of “bleh.”

You can find the Lufthansa A350-1000 seat map here.

Lufthansa Airbus A350-1000s will all be stationed in Munich (MUC), which is where Lufthansa bases all of its A350s. The first of these planes is entering long haul commercial service as of early December 2026.

Specifically, as of December 3, 2026, the A350-1000 will fly between Munich and Tokyo Haneda (HND), with the next two destinations being Shanghai (PVG) and Singapore (SIN), and those services expected to launch within weeks, though the schedule hasn’t yet been updated to reflect that.

Note that initially the flights won’t be operated by the A350-1000 daily, so there will be alternating service with the A350-900. It’s interesting that the initial route isn’t to North America, where a single plane could do a same day turn, and continuously stay in service. but I guess there’s enough commonality between the A350-900 and A350-1000, so it’s not a big deal.

As far as US destinations go, it’s expected that Chicago (ORD) and Newark (EWR) will be the first two cities to see the new plane, though there’s no exact timeline for that yet.

In 2023, Lufthansa placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000, and the first of these planes has just been delivered, and will enter service in early December 2026. The plane features 300 seats across four cabins, though still only expect one row of first class seats. The Munich-based plane will initially fly to Tokyo, Shanghai, and Singapore. I must say, Lufthansa knocked it out of the park with its centennial livery, and I can’t wait to see this plane flying.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s Airbus A350-1000 deliveries?

AI is all set to take delivery of VT-JRP some time in November 2026, so it will be a tight race as to whether D-AIFA or VT-JRP enters service first. #6170. Midterm Mayhem for the Free and Virtuous Society

The GOP will continue to suffer at the polls until it focuses on building this type of society once again.

President Donald Trump speaks in front of a portrait of Ronald Reagan at the White House in Washington, D.C., March 24, 2026.

There has been some pretty unsurprising but bad analysis of the election results since Tuesday night. There also has been some very good analysis, from National Review’s editors, from our own Jim Geraghty, from our own Dan McLaughlin, from Yuval Levin, from Erick Erickson, and plenty of others on the conservative right. There is no need for a redundant analysis that merely restates what has already been said, even though an amen to all of what they said should be assumed. What I want to suggest, in total alignment with my aforementioned friends and colleagues, is that these election results capture the very essence of the twin deficits in the Trump-era moment: a newfound contempt for both the free and the virtuous society.

The debate over the Iran war’s role in this Republican debacle would be comical if it were not so maddening. With virtually no one operating in good faith or making a serious argument, a whole cabal of people have claimed, all statistical evidence and voter polling to the contrary, that the sole reason for states like Texas, Kansas, and Mississippi flipping is the Iran war. Inversely, no one who disputes that monocausal theory of the case denies that the Iran war is unpopular, and that its unpopularity was a contributor to the decline of approval for President Trump and to the results Republicans suffered all over the country Tuesday night. That voters detest the state of prices, and that they believe (with obvious basis in fact) that tariffs are connected to this, is not disputable by credible people. That the bizarre handling of the Iran war led to a Strait of Hormuz debacle, and to significant problems for fuel prices and a downstream impact from diesel prices, is also obvious. Reasonable people can disagree as to how much of the Iran war contribution was related to opposition to de-nuclearizing Iran versus the way in which it all went (e.g., a failed MOU negotiated by the vice president, repeated claims of victory that were obviously untrue, and a sustained period of time with no clear resolution). But all advocates of a multi-causal explanation of the midterms recognize the significant role Iran played.

David L. Bahnsen is the managing partner of a wealth-management firm and a frequent writer and public commentator on matters of economics, faith and work, and markets.

#6169. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

#6168. Back From The Desert: How 190 Airbus A380s Became Airlines' Most Valuable Asset In 2026

The Airbus A380 is a unique aircraft in many ways, and is one of commercial aviation's greatest success stories, beloved by passengers worldwide. At the same time, it is also one of the largest commercial failures in modern aviation, especially for its manufacturer Airbus.

Over the course of the aircraft's production, 251 units were delivered to airlines, before the program was discontinued in 2021 after less than two decades due to a lack of commercial interest. For Airbus, the program never reached the break-even point, resulting in an estimated sunken cost of up to 25 billion dollars, making the A380 one of the most unprofitable aircraft in aviation history.

The Airbus A380 is undoubtedly one of the most iconic aircraft ever built, and is the only full-length double-decker aircraft in operations. On the 27th of April 2026, it has been 21 years since the Airbus A380 departed on its first-ever flight. Since the aircraft's first commercial flight in 2007 with Singapore Airlines, the type has flown over 800,000 flights carrying more than 300 million passengers. At the time of the aircraft's first flight, few would have believed that less than two decades later, in December 2021, Airbus would deliver the last A380 ever built to Emirates.

After the aircraft successfully entered commercial service in 2007, production peaked in 2012, with 30 new aircraft being constructed. However, by 2021, in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, Airbus made the decision to discontinue production of the aircraft after less than two decades, as the A380 did not succeed in the modern aviation market on a large enough scale. Unsurprisingly, this short production period was not enough to recover the massive development costs of the aircraft.

An important factor resulting in airlines' lack of interest for the A380 was that Airbus introduced the aircraft too late, and the market had already evolved. While Airbus had already started studies to develop the aircraft back in 1988, the market was already shifting away from the "hubs-and-spokes" model the aircraft was designed for by the time it was first delivered in 2007. Airlines were already increasingly opting for smaller and more efficient twin-jet aircraft such as the Airbus' own A350 and Boeing 787. These aircraft fitted better in this shifting commercial aviation market, and allowed airlines to operate more direct long-haul routes with thinner demand.

For Airbus, the final setback to the A380 program came when the type's largest customer, Emirates, decided to cancel and switch a large part of their outstanding order in favor of the smaller A350 and Boeing 777X. This made the already troubled program completely unviable for Airbus, ultimately resulting in the final blow ending the aircraft production. For Emirates, an important reason to switch to smaller, more versatile aircraft came as Airbus could not deliver on a more fuel-efficient version of the A380, a potential "A380neo". Despite this, Emirates still values the aircraft and expects to operate it into the next decade.

Production peaked in the early 2010s before orders dropped off.

Despite production ending in 2021, the aircraft remains a valuable asset for some airlines. These airlines often use the aircraft on high-demand hub routes with consistent demand to fill the large number of seats on the aircraft. These large hub airports are often heavily capacity-constrained, limiting growth possibilities in the number of flights and forcing airlines to increase aircraft size instead. Doing so allows airlines to maximize passengers per slot and capture more revenue on limited frequencies. In addition, most airlines have, for at least a large part, paid off their A380s or leased them at lower rates, decreasing ownership costs. This can make the aircraft an even more attractive asset, provided an airline's route network has enough high-demand "trunk" routes.

Furthermore, the A380 still has a leading passenger experience due to its spacious cabin, stable flight, and low noise levels. For airlines, the spacious cabin is particularly interesting as it allows for the installation of premium heavy cabins and to design industry-leading, flagship premium products, such as first-class suites, as well as onboard showers and bars. Something that is especially attractive for airlines with premium-heavy revenue models.

Underscoring the strategic value of the aircraft for some airlines became clear at the 2023 Dubai Air Show, when Emirates announced a 1.5 billion dollar investment plan to make its A380 ready for the next decade. At the time of the announcement, Sir Tim Clark, President of Emirates, said the following:

“The A380 has been and will continue to be very much part of the Emirates story. Its size and capacity has allowed Emirates to unlock growth at some of the world’s busiest airports, opened new opportunities for travelers, and substantially raised standards for passenger comfort.”

What do you think is the real reason Airbus discontinued the A380?

Around the world, there are ten airlines operating about 190 Airbus A380 aircraft. The most famous and largest operator of the aircraft type is Emirates. In fact, Emirates' A380 fleet is so large that it accounts for more than half of the total A380 fleet worldwide, with 116 aircraft. The next largest operators of the A380 are British Airways and the type's launch customer Singapore Airlines, which both operate 12 A380s. Other operators in the top five include Australian flag carrier Qantas with 10 aircraft, and Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, which currently operates nine aircraft, after having recently reactivated two additional aircraft of the type that had previously been stored.

Other notable operators of the aircraft include Lufthansa (8), Qatar Airways (8), Korean Air (6) and sister-airline Asiana (6). The last airline to welcome the A380 to its fleet was Japanese carrier All Nippon Airlines (ANA), which added the aircraft to its fleet back in 2019, a decision the airline probably regrets as the massive capacity of the A380 quickly became a hurdle when market conditions changed. As of writing, ANA operates three A380s, which exclusively serve the Japan to Hawaii market. Another honorable mention is the ambitious and ambiguous Global Airlines, which briefly began operations in the summer of 2025, leasing an A380 from Malta-based charter airline Hi Fly Malta.

Source: planespotters.net (As of April 2026)

The airlines that opted to retain the A380 in their fleets have clearly done so with conviction and are investing heavily in the aircraft. This illustrates clearly that airlines are not operating the aircraft out of convenience or as a cash cow, but rather see it as a long-term strategic asset. In December 2025, for example, Qantas welcomed back its tenth and final A380 to Sydney after having been in storage for almost six years. To get the aircraft back into service, more than 100,000 hours of work were done by engineering and maintenance teams along with a full cabin retrofit, marking the largest maintenance check in the airline's history.

And it is not only Qantas investing in the aircraft. As mentioned earlier, Emirates is investing over a billion dollars into retrofitting the aircraft, future-proofing it for the next decade. And also, German flag carrier Lufthansa is investing heavily in its A380 fleet, retrofitting the aircraft's cabin as the airline decided to operate the A380 into the 2030s since a true replacement for the aircraft is not available and deliveries of new twinjets are facing delays.

A look at the challenges of operating a fleet of Airbus A380s today, and the future outlook on the type.

For airlines, one of the biggest problems with large aircraft, such as the A380, is the simple fact that high load factors are a requirement to be efficient. When a 500-seat aircraft flies half empty, its fuel burn per seat rises quickly, whereas smaller aircraft can match demand better and avoid overcapacity. Since only a few routes have sufficient demand to consistently fill the aircraft, airlines are limited in terms of viable routes they can deploy the aircraft on. Besides the economics, the aircraft also comes with a number of operational inefficiencies for airlines. These include infrastructure requirements at airports, increased turnaround times, and perhaps most notably, the increased maintenance cost due to the aircraft's four engines.

While a number of airlines worldwide clearly view the A380 as a valuable asset, beneficial enough to be worthwhile, several others retired the aircraft years ago. These include Air France (10), which was the first airline to fully retire the aircraft, as well as China Southern Airways (5), Thai Airways (6), and Malaysia Airlines (6). For most of these airlines, the aircraft were already planned to be retired due to the high operating costs, with the pandemic accelerating the retirement in most cases.

Besides these airlines that have completely retired their A380s, a number of current operators mentioned earlier have also temporarily or partially grounded or retired the sub-fleet already. For example, launch customer Singapore Airlines has already retired half of its original A380 fleet, while Etihad Airways even temporarily grounded its entire fleet. The same also goes for Lufthansa, Qantas, and Qatar Airways having temporarily parked and later retired a portion of their superjumbo fleet.

#6167. A350-1000ULR Sets New Distance Record

Airbus’ A350-1000ULR has been officially recognized for breaking the Guinness World Record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial aircraft.

The record-breaking flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France, took place in July and was widely reported on, but was only recently confirmed by Guinness using data validated by the International Aeronautical Federation and flightradar24.

The nonstop journey covered 12,503 nautical miles and lasted 24 hours and 24 minutes. The -1000ULR flew over Sydney and the Pacific on a north-easterly routing toward Los Angeles, crossed North America and the Atlantic, and passed over London on its way to Toulouse. According to Airbus, the 13 people on board witnessed two sunsets and two sunrises.

The crew included three Airbus flight test pilots, two pilots from Qantas, and five Airbus flight test engineers. Also on board were two Airbus design engineers and a representative from the IAF.

Airbus is developing the -1000ULR for Qantas’ Project Sunrise, a yearslong effort to connect the east coast of Australia with far-flung destinations such as New York and London. The manufacturer expects to deliver the first of the type in April 2027. Qantas is aiming to operate the first Project Sunrise flight, from Sydney to London, later that year.

The Australian flag carrier has ordered 12 -1000ULRs.

“In responding to the challenge laid down by Qantas, our teams came together to extend the range of the A350-1000 in an efficient and economically viable way to undertake the world’s longest ever commercial flights,” Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus, said in a news release. “Flying 12,503 nautical miles non-stop, we have fully proven the aircraft’s capability to fulfill its mission. And the world record was the icing on the cake.”

Many airlines, hotels, theme parks and cruise lines pay year-round tribute to military service members with generous discounts and benefits. Sometimes these deals are available only to active-duty military personnel, and at other times the perks extend to U.S. military veterans and their families.

Related: The best credit cards for active-duty military members: Get waived annual fees

No matter the form these military travel deals take, they all reflect the gratitude the travel industry feels toward those who have sacrificed so much to protect our country.

Here are the perks that military members can take advantage of on their travels in 2026.

To honor military members, B Hotels & Resorts offers an exclusive “B Saluted” discount of 15% off regular rates for military members, veterans and their families. Florida-based B Hotels & Resorts has locations in Fort Lauderdale and Marathon.

Through the "Honoring Our Heroes" program, Sandals and Beaches resorts in Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Antigua, the Bahamas, Grenada, Barbados, Curacao, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines offer a 10% discount to eligible U.S. military members and veterans.

Best Western properties across the U.S. offer discounted rates for veterans, military members and government personnel.

Best Western’s Service Rewards program — the hotel chain’s free award program tailored to military and armed forces members — unlocks even more member benefits, including an automatic upgrade to Gold status and bonus points on qualified stays.

In November, military members can receive 10% off their stay at Big Cedar Lodge, as well as 25% off resort activities including a spa day pass, golf simulators, bowling and more.

Through the Waves4Warriors Club, CheapCaribbean Vacations offers active-duty service members, veterans and military families access to exclusive deals, room upgrades, special perks and savings of $150 off a qualifying five-night or longer vacation package after you join at hotel brands including Breathless, Dreams, Zoetry, Royalton and more.

Choice Hotels — including Comfort, Sleep Inn and Quality Inn hotels — offers discounted rates for official and leisure travel to active-duty and retired military personnel, their dependents and members of several military associations. When you are searching for a hotel, open the drop-down "Rate" menu and choose "Military/Veterans (Leisure)" for leisure travel or "Government/Military (Official Business Travel)" for work travel.

Active-duty military members, veterans and military spouses are eligible to join the Choice Privileges rewards program at the Gold Elite level.

Extended Stay America offers discounted rates to military members at three brands and more than 650 locations across the U.S. To receive the discount, choose "Government & Military" from the dropdown box during booking.

Great Wolf Lodge offers up to 40% off nightly rates for active, retired and veteran military members through the Howling Heroes offer. The offer is valid for up to two guests per room, with a $20 fee per additional guest.

The Grove Resort & Water Park is a one-stop hotel and water park only a short drive from Walt Disney World. Military members can receive up to 20% off the best available rate when booking through this link.

Federal and U.S. military employees qualify for military rates and discounts at participating Hilton properties. There are separate discounts for official and leisure military travel. For official military travel, check the box labeled “Government and military rates” to apply the rates. For leisure travel, visit Hilton's Military Family Rate page and search for your travel destination and dates.

Veterans, active-duty members and their immediate family members are eligible for a discount of 10%-15% off Hyatt’s standard rate at participating U.S. hotels. To get the discount, use the offer code "MILVET" while booking.

The hotel chain behind brands such as InterContinental, Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza and Kimpton offers a military rate at participating locations worldwide. The rate applies to active-duty military personnel, veterans, retired military personnel and their families.

Margaritaville Beach Resort's "Salute to Heroes" rate offers up to a 35% discount to active-duty service members and veterans.

Marriott Bonvoy offers discounted federal, state and local government rates available to government and military personnel. To access the discounted rates, choose the “Government & Military” option from the “Special Rates” drop-down menu when searching for a stay. You’ll get a list of all the Marriott Bonvoy properties in your chosen city that offer special rates and their eligibility requirements.

Motel 6, along with its sister extended-stay brand Studio 6, offers a 10% discount on standard rates to active and retired military personnel.

Active-duty military personnel, veterans and government employees are eligible for a 10% discount on official travel at any U.S. Red Roof location. The hotel chain also has a 10% discount on leisure travel for all government employees and military members, veterans and retirees.

If you are traveling to Hawaii for military business or leisure, The Surfjack offers a range of military discounts. With the "Get Shacked @ The Jack" promotion, military members can save 25% on room rates, bring a pet for free and receive discounts on dining and parking.

TradeWinds Resort in St. Pete Beach, Florida, offers up to 25% off its best available rates to military members when you use code "Military" at booking.

Participating Wyndham properties offer discounts of up to 15% off their best available rate to active and retired military personnel, veterans and their families. Plus, qualifying military personnel and their spouses get automatic Gold status when they enroll in the Wyndham Rewards program and bonus Wyndham Rewards points for qualified stays.

In some markets, Alaska Airlines offers discounted military fares to active-duty military personnel and their dependents when you call 800-252-7522 to purchase your tickets. The airline also offers discounts through the WeSalute+ program.

Active-duty U.S. military personnel can board early, check up to five bags for free, receive 15% off inflight food purchases and receive complimentary day passes to visit an Alaska Lounge when traveling on official government-sponsored travel. All other active-duty military personnel can purchase a discounted lounge day pass for $40.

U.S. active-duty and reserve military members, military veterans, members of the National Guard and their dependents get up to two pieces of checked baggage for free through the Allegiant Honors program. Also, the airline waives its typical fees for oversized checked baggage, a carry-on bag, getting a boarding pass printed at the airport, bringing a pet on board, seat assignments and change or cancellation fees due to a change in orders or directives. Qualifying service members can also board their flights early.

American Airlines offers government or military fares in some markets, but you must call the airline at 800-433-7300 to book. Veterans and their families can access reduced fares by enrolling in the WeSalute+ program.

Active-duty military personnel are also allowed Group 1 boarding privileges, and they can bring up to five free checked bags when traveling on orders and up to three free checked bags when traveling for leisure (weight restrictions apply).

U.S. military personnel traveling in uniform on a same-day American flight can enter Admirals Club lounges with their immediate family — defined as a spouse, domestic partner and/or children under 18 — or up to two guests at most Admirals Club locations except for Airspace Lounge at San Diego International Airport (SAN) and Japan Airlines' Sakura Lounge at Honolulu’s Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL).

Active-duty U.S. service members can call Delta Reservations at 800-221-1212 for discounted fares unavailable to the general public. Delta also offers priority boarding and free checked baggage to active-duty military members. The number of bags you are allowed depends on the type of travel and fare type, and you must adhere to the specified baggage size and weight restrictions.

Frontier typically charges for carry-on bags and checked baggage. However, active-duty armed forces, National Guard and Reserve members, their accompanying spouse and children can receive a free carry-on bag, two free checked bags and one free personal item.

Active-duty military personnel traveling for business or leisure are eligible for a 5% discount on base fares. If traveling on government-sponsored business, call 800-538-2583 to receive your discount and up to five free checked bags (military members traveling for leisure get up to two free checked bags). This discount applies to you and your immediate family.

U.S. active-duty military members, retired military members, veterans, National Guard and Reserve members, and their families enrolled in WeSalute+ can also get a 5% discount on base fares and up to two free checked bags.

Special fares are available for military and government travelers, but you must call the airline at 800-435-9792 or visit the airport ticket counter to book them. Additionally, military members traveling on active duty receive priority boarding before Group 1 and are exempt from the two-piece baggage limit.

United offers an additional checked baggage allowance, priority boarding and United Club lounge access to active-duty military members traveling in uniform. U.S. military veterans, active-duty military members, National Guard and Reserve members, and their families are also eligible for a 5% discount on United-operated flights.

Active-duty U.S. military personnel, spouses and dependents are eligible for a 10% discount on the lowest available fare in select fare classes. Select “Military” for each eligible passenger during your ticket search on Fare Finder. Amtrak also welcomes uniformed military personnel to the front of the ticket line.

All U.S. SeaWorld, Busch Gardens, Aquatica and Sesame Place parks offer discounted tickets to active-duty military members and veterans through the Waves of Honor program. Most parks also offer at least one complimentary admission per year.

Disneyland honors active and retired U.S. military personnel with discounted one-, three- and four-day Disney Military Promotional tickets. The three- and four-day tickets include access to Disneyland and Disney California Adventure each day of your ticket, while the one-day ticket is good for entry to one park only (excluding blackout dates). Pricing starts at $98, and you must purchase tickets at a participating U.S. military base ticket office or through govx.com. Theme park reservations are required.

Hotel discounts are also available by calling 866-309-9737.

Dollywood offers discounted tickets and annual passes to U.S. active or retired military members, veterans, military reservists, spouses and dependents.

Military members who visit the home of America's first president can save $4 on admission tickets, while Purple Heart recipients and active-duty members in uniform receive free admission all year long. Every year on Veterans Day, however, all active-duty, former or retired military personnel receive free admission and can participate in an annual tribute by placing a flower on General Washington's tomb.

Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, offers discounted daily tickets and season passes to active, retired and veteran military members. To access this discount, purchase online or present your government ID at the park's ticket booth.

Most U.S.-based Merlin Entertainments attractions offer discounted military tickets, but a handful of locations are giving away free tickets to military members and veterans through Nov. 30. These include Legoland parks in Florida and New York, Madame Tussauds Orlando and Sea Life Aquariums in Orlando, Grapevine, Texas, Kansas City, Missouri, and San Antonio, Texas.

Active duty and retired military personnel and veterans, along with their spouses and dependents, can purchase a Military Passport season pass starting at $119.99.Silver Dollar City also offers a ticket discount to U.S. active or retired military personnel, veterans and military reservists, along with their spouses and dependent children (ages 4-17) living in their households.

In addition to discounted tickets, Silver Dollar City invites all military members and veterans to help raise the American flag during the park’s daily opening ceremony. Service members are also given a red, white and blue ribbon to wear in the park, allowing employees and guests to thank them for their service.

St. Augustine has hundreds of years of military history, much of which you can still visit today. The city shows its appreciation to military service members year-round with discounts on accommodations, attractions and experiences.

Universal Orlando offers a Military Freedom Pass promotional ticket to all active-duty and retired service members. Ticket prices start at $220 for unlimited admission between now and Dec.18, 2026, though blackout dates apply. Each eligible service member can purchase up to six promotional tickets and must buy them through a participating authorized military ticket and travel office. Military members can also purchase discounted tickets to the new Universal Epic Universe park.

Universal Studios Hollywood offers discounted tickets to active-duty, retired and eligible veteran military members, along with their spouses and dependents. Additional on-base discounts are available, including a 12-month Military Pass.

Active and retired U.S. military personnel are eligible for discounted hotel rates and specially priced theme park tickets at Walt Disney World. Military members can purchase a Military Salute ticket with either Park Hopper or Park Hopper Plus starting at $409 for a four-day ticket, $429 for a five-day ticket and $449 for a six-day ticket. Disney World also offers a special ticket valid for multiple visits through Dec. 18, 2026, starting at $499.

Blackout dates apply, and theme park reservations are required. Hotel stays can be booked by calling 407-939-7830. Tickets must be purchased at a participating U.S. military base ticket office to avoid being charged a sales tax, but are also available at Disney World ticket windows.

Vail Resorts offers Epic Military Passes for active-duty service members, retired military members and veterans. Prices start at just $230 for unlimited skiing at more than 40 Vail Resorts and discounts on family passes, food, lodging, gear rentals and more.

AmaWaterways offers active and retired service members a special military discount of $250 per person off a river cruise or enjoy two-for-one cruise fares on select 2026 and 2027 sailings when you use the code "MIL250" or "MIL2FOR1" when booking.

Carnival Cruise Line shows its appreciation for active and retired members of the armed forces with discounted cruise rates, onboard credits and reduced deposits. Additionally, some ships have a Heroes Tribute Lounge, and every ship holds a military appreciation gathering for service members and their families.

On select Celebrity Cruises sailings, active and retired military members can save $25 on inside and ocean-view cabins and $100 on veranda cabins and above, and these savings can be combined with other current promotions. This discount applies to the first and second guests in the cabin.

Disney Cruise Line offers special rates to all military members, active and retired, and their spouses. Discounted rates are only available on select sailings. To honor America's 250th anniversary, the cruise line is offering a $250 onboard credit for eligible U.S. military personnel on select Disney Wish and Disney Dream sailings in 2026.

MSC Cruises offers discounted fares to all active and retired U.S. military personnel, as well as family members traveling with them. You can receive a discount of 5% on interior and ocean-view cabins, 10% on balcony and suite cabins, and a “kids sail free” promotion on select sailings.

Margaritaville at Sea honors active and veteran military members with a free cruise through the Heroes Sail Free program. On select sailings, military members and an additional guest in the same cabin can get a free fare (taxes and fees are not included). A third and fourth guest can be added at the regular fare. On all other sailings, military members can save 20% off the retail fare for the first four guests in the cabin.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Military Appreciation program extends exclusive benefits to military members, veterans and their spouses. Members of the program receive up to a 20% discount on select sailings.

Veterans and active, retired and disabled military personnel can receive up to $250 free onboard spending money on select Princess Cruises sailings. You can use this onboard credit for specialty dining, onboard boutiques, shore excursions, spa treatments and more.

Royal Caribbean offers military rates to active and retired personnel, veterans and their spouses. The discounted rates also apply to friends and family members staying in the same cabin as the eligible service member. The best way to access the discounted rate is to book through a travel agent or to book directly with Royal Caribbean over the phone.

A host of benefits awaits travelers who have served or are serving in the U.S. military.

Because these military travel deals, their requirements, and the eligibility of family members, spouses and dependents vary, carefully research each military discount offer to avoid surprises. Many airlines, hotels and other businesses might ask for proof of eligibility, so don’t leave home without the military ID, veteran ID, dependent ID, orders and/or other documentation you’ll need to take advantage of the many travel offers.

#6165. Airline Interline, Codeshare, Alliance, And Joint Venture Agreements Explained

Airline partnerships are more complex and advanced than ever before, both for better and worse. About 25 years ago the Star Alliance was formed, which was revolutionary at the time. SkyTeam and oneworld quickly joined the scene.

While they all still exist, the global alliances have definitely been deemphasized a bit in recent years. After all, with these alliances having so many members, how much can loosely affiliated airlines really have in common?

Airlines want to work with other airlines that complement them best, and this can come in many different forms. Just to give a few examples of partnerships outside of the traditional alliances:

Airlines have several different levels of cooperation, ranging from interline agreements, to codeshare agreements, to alliance membership, to joint venture agreements. In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the differences between these agreements. Before I do so, let me add two disclaimers:

With that out of the way, let’s take a look at these four kinds of agreements.

Interline agreements are the most basic kinds of agreements you can have between airlines. An interline agreement is simply a commercial agreement between airlines to handle passengers when they’re traveling on multiple airlines on the same itinerary, and it allows an airline to issue a ticket on another airline (though not necessarily on any sort of favorable commercial terms).

This allows passengers to check their bags through to their final destination, get boarding passes all way to their destination, potentially be rebooked on another airline in the event of irregular operations, etc.

This is a basic level of cooperation, so there are airlines that have interline agreements but don’t otherwise have robust partnerships. For example, Etihad doesn’t belong to a major global alliance, but has an interline agreement with dozens of airlines, ranging from American, to Emirates, to JetBlue, to United, to Qatar Airways.

As you can see, this is a level of cooperation we even see between airlines that don’t partner with one another, and that may not even be fond of one another.

It is worth noting that in some cases airlines specifically pull out of interline agreements. For example, many years ago Delta cut its interline agreement with American. Why? At least in part it’s because Delta found that American was rebooking more passengers on Delta during irregular operations than the other way around, so the carrier no longer thought the arrangement was in its best interest.

A codeshare agreement is the next level of cooperation between airlines. This is when two airlines realize there’s value in working together, and they decide they want to place their “codes” on one another’s flights. Typically the main benefit of this is that it drums up business for the airlines that are in a codeshare agreement with one another.

Just to give an example, Alaska Airlines and Icelandair have a codeshare agreement. Icelandair flies to certain gateways in the United States, and then Alaska Airlines provides some of the “feed” for those flights in the form of codeshares.

For example, if you want to fly from Reykjavik to Los Angeles, Icelandair doesn’t operate that route. However, Icelandair flies to Portland, and then you can book a Portland to Los Angeles flight on Alaska Airlines as an Icelandair codeshare.

When you book a codeshare flight, you’ll notice that the flight number is different. So if you booked through Icelandair, your Portland to Los Angeles flight would also have an Icelandair flight number (in this case FI7696). To be clear:

With these codeshare agreements, generally neither airline is getting a huge cut for booking someone on the other airline. Most of the ticket revenue goes to the operating carrier, and often a small amount goes to the airline that sold the flight. However, the biggest advantage of this arrangement is to boost business for both airlines by increasing the number of flights that passengers have access to.

The “big three” alliances — oneworld, SkyTeam, and Star Alliance — have only developed in the past 25 years, though in the meantime many major global carriers belong to one of them. The basic way that alliances work is as follows:

I’d note that different airlines place different levels of emphasis on these alliances, even if they choose to belong to them. For example, Delta is a founding member of SkyTeam, but the airline is heavily focused on joint ventures and airlines it owns a stake in, and cares very little about the airlines it simply shares an alliance with.

If a codeshare agreement is like dating, then a joint venture is like getting married. A joint venture agreement is a massive business decision that typically requires extensive government approval. When airlines form a joint venture they coordinate pricing and schedules, and have a revenue sharing agreement.

Exactly how the revenue sharing works depends on the specific arrangement, but the idea is that two airlines are essentially acting as one under a joint venture.

Note that typically airlines form joint ventures between specific regions, which is why this is different than an outright merger. For example, American has a transatlantic joint venture with British Airways, Finnair, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, while the airline has two transpacific joint ventures, with both Japan Airlines and Qantas (the two are separate arrangements).

From the perspective of a consumer, a joint venture is both good and bad. The good news is that typically it gives you the most flight options in terms of schedules, since the airlines are operating as one. Airlines also often try to make the experience as consistent across brands as possible. The downside is that it’s like a competitor being eliminated in the market, so it could lead to higher fares as it reduces competition.

There are so many different types of agreements in the airline industry nowadays. While the exact terms vary with every partnership, I think the easiest way to sum it up is that an interline agreement is like a friendship, a codeshare agreement is like an engagement, a joint venture is like a marriage, and an alliance is like having a big family, with everyone sort of doing their own thing.

There’s a lot more to all of this, but hopefully the above provides a pretty fair and basic summary. People often misuse these terms, so I figure it’s worth recapping every so often.

#6164. Lufthansa Takes Delivery of Its First A350-1000

Lufthansa this week took delivery of its first Airbus A350-1000, a type it says will offer a better customer experience while reducing operating costs.

The aircraft was formally handed over to the carrier on Tuesday in the presence of Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr and Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus. Nicknamed “Deutschland,” the jet is Lufthansa’s 700th Airbus airplane, and the seventh in a special commemorative fleet bearing 100th anniversary liveries.

The white and dark blue designs feature an oversized crane, a symbol first used by predecessor Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa Group has ordered a total of 15 A350-1000s. The first 10 will operate for the Lufthansa core brand, and will be based at its Munich hub.

“Deutschland” will fly to Munich on Wednesday, officials said, and operate its inaugural flight, to Tokyo-Haneda, on Dec. 3. The aircraft will also be Lufthansa’s first long-haul airplane equipped with Starlink satellite internet service.

“The fact that, as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus aircraft exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa, and in the year of our 100th anniversary, makes this a very special moment for us,” Spohr said in a statement. “Our partnership is a prime example of what Europe can achieve when it works together.”

Lufthansa’s -1000s will seat 300 passengers in four cabins – First, Business, Premium Economy, and Economy.

#6163. Plaza Premium Opening Hong Kong Arrivals Lounge… With Live Music?!

Plaza Premium will be opening an arrivals lounge soon at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG). While these facilities are always useful for a shower and breakfast after an overnight flight, it sounds like there might be a bit more planned for this arrivals lounge? I’m certainly intrigued (thanks to Sel_D for flagging this)…

Plaza Premium is expected to open an arrivals lounge at Hong Kong Airport in late November 2026. The lounge will be located on level three of Terminal 2, in the arrivals portion of the terminal, below the Airport Express platform. That means it’ll be landside.

This actually technically represents the reopening of a lounge, as the global lounge operator had such a facility until 2019. At that point it closed due to an expansion project at the airport. Once open, it will be the only arrivals lounge at the airport. Cathay Pacific used to have an arrivals lounge at its hub, but it closed in 2018, and the airline has no plans to reopen such a facility.

The exact entry requirements of the Plaza Premium arrivals lounge in Hong Kong remain to be seen, but like most Plaza Premium lounges, the expectation is that entry will be possible through select credit cards and Priority Pass, and access can also be purchased directly.

Generally we think of an arrivals lounge in terms of its functional purpose, which is to shower, have breakfast, and get some work done, before heading into the city. Many arrivals lounges are only open in the morning, since that’s when there’s the most value. That’s especially true for people who either plan to head to the office, or who are staying at a hotel, where it’s well before the published check-in time.

While it remains to be seen what exactly Plaza Premium’s facility will be like, it sounds like this will be a rather unconventional arrivals lounge, in a good way. The social media post about the new lounge describes it as “Plaza Premium Lounge – Rhythms.” It will offer a “seamless blend of dining, music, wellness, and refreshment.”

In terms of the range of amenities, we’re being promised live music, wellness experiences, refined dining, and private resting spaces. I’m sorry… live music? Like… someone performing music live? In an arrivals lounge? Fascinatingly, the pictures make it look more like an evening-oriented lounge serving cocktails and wine, for lounging around, rather than your typical arrivals lounge.

A post shared by Plaza Premium Lounge (@plazapremiumlounge)

Suffice it to say that I am very interested in what they come up with here. From a monetization standpoint, this seems kind of smart, since it could drum up more business in the afternoons and evenings, when people might not otherwise consider visiting such a facility. Then again, are people really thinking “I just got off a 15 hour flight, what I could really use is a cocktail before heading to my hotel?” Maybe they are, I suppose!

In the coming weeks, Hong Kong Airport will once again have an arrivals lounge, thanks to the opening of a facility by Plaza Premium. Arrivals lounges are usually pretty basic, and are about showers and breakfast. While we’ll see how much of this is fluff rather than actual substance, Plaza Premium is promising what sounds more like a bar vibe, with live music and cocktails. Bring it on, Plaza Premium, I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of this Plaza Premium concept?
