#6162. The Runway Grooves That Help Commercial Jets Stop During Heavy Rain

RonaldoSoffel | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The United States helped to pioneer runway grooving in an attempt to improve aircraft traction and water drainage. NASA's Wallops research runway carried out almost 200 braking tests with a McDonnell Douglas F-4D Phantom II fighter and a four-engine Convair 990 airliner.

It was found that grooves substantially increase the braking capability of heavy jet-powered aircraft on wet, flooded, and slushy surfaces. Over the history of aviation, a variety of runway cuts were used, including square grooves, V-shaped grooves, and trapezoidal grooves. Eventually, the FAA settled on the straight-line grooves common at airports today.

However, grooves are not the only way to achieve sufficient traction, with their effectiveness waxing and waning depending on the climate and other factors. Overall, it appears the worldwide trend in the 2010s and 2020s is for grooved runways to become more common, although it is difficult to quantify.

Some roadways, certain footpaths, and some runways have small grooves cut across them to improve traction and water drainage. These are designed to give rainwater a way out from under an aircraft's tires and to improve its traction. The key issue they are designed to solve is hydroplaning. At high enough speeds on a wet runway, an aircraft's tire footprint can lift off the pavement and ride on a layer of water.

Typical FAA specifications for transverse grooves are approximately 1/4 inch (6.4 mm) in width and depth and 1.5 inches (38 mm) in spacing. A 1997 FAA Advisory Circular titled 'Measurement, Construction, and Maintenance of Skid-Resistant Airport Pavement Surfaces' noted that:

"With the introduction of turbojet aircraft, braking performance on pavement surfaces has become more critical. Under certain conditions, hydroplaning or unacceptable loss of traction can occur, resulting in poor braking performance and possible loss of directional control."

It adds that NASA, the FAA, the USAF, and various foreign governments conducted a series of research projects that concentrated on two main areas. One was high skid-resistant pavement, and the other was "application of proper maintenance techniques and procedures." It asserts that runway grooves are a proven and effective technique for providing skid resistance and preventing hydroplaning during wet weather.

The 1997 FAA paper discusses the grooving techniques. These include cutting or forming grooves in existing or new pavement. Grooves in new PCC pavement need to be formed while the concrete is still plastic, while grooves in HMA pavement need to be saw-cut. It said that all runways that served or were expected to serve turbojet aircraft were considered a high priority for grooving.

Existing runways without grooving also had to be modified as soon as practical. The paper noted that some existing pavements may have surfaces that are now suitable for sawing grooves. It recommended that studies should be done to determine whether they could be overlaid or rehabilitated to allow grooving.

The need for grooves on runways that do not serve turbojets was not automatic and depended on circumstances. As mentioned below, this does not apply to US Navy or Air Force runways used by commercial airlines.

FAA groove specifications for transverse grooves (per FAA)

1.5 inches (3.8 cm) apart, center to center

Today, grooving is very common around the world at major commercial airports, although it is not fully universal (even among major international airports). Grooving at general aviation airports is considerably less common. It is particularly common in commercial airports in the United States, partly due to the FAA taking a particularly strong position on the matter.

Oceanic airspace is a challenging place to be, far away from civilization and communication outposts. Before entering, pilots reduce speed, but why?

In Europe and other international airports, grooving may be less common than in the United States. ICAO's international standards are less prescriptive than the FAA's, although it recognizes grooving as a way to improve wet-runway braking. It stops short of making conventional grooving universally mandatory.

Europe's EASA sees grooving as one possible method to improve runway friction and surface texture. Canada's Transportation Safety Board states that grooving reduces the potential for both dynamic and viscous hydroplaning by providing a place (such as grooves) where water can escape from underneath tires.

However, it explicitly states that "runway grooving is not a requirement for new or existing runway pavement in Canada." The FAA paper above was published in 1997, but it wasn't until 2013 that Ottawa International Airport became the first airport in Canada to groove its runway. Despite being often wet, Canada is a strong example that has historically resisted mandated grooving.

Instead, it has been content to leave it as an option. China is an example of a country that prefers alternative treatments such as stone mastic asphalt and other textured pavement surfaces. France also uses specialized asphalt surfacing as an alternative. A 2010 Canadian safety investigation found that grooving is present at almost all major airports in the US, UK, continental Europe, Australia, and Japan.

Most small general aviation airports do not have grooved runways, and this is driven by several practical reasons. One is that light aircraft have a lower landing weight and speed than commercial airlines and so are less susceptible to hydroplaning. Another is that low traffic volume may not justify the costs of grooving.

Engineers often assess that these airports are built with pavement characteristics that already provide adequate friction and drainage without the need for grooves. Some airports achieve adequate wet-weather friction through alternative surface treatments. These include porous friction course.

Here, a porous asphalt overlay allows water drainage, concrete texturing, surface aggregate selection, and runway gradients. With concrete texturing, concrete can be finished with wire combing or tining, creating a textured surface. General aviation aircraft are actually quite vulnerable to runway skidding and hydroplaning, but grooving is not necessarily seen as the way to address this.

Much of the issue stems from light aircraft often lacking anti-skid braking systems, operating from shorter and less frequently maintained runways, and their relatively small tires. Without anti-skid braking, if a pilot applies too much braking on a slippery surface, the wheels can lock and skid. After a wheel locks, its braking effectiveness tends to deteriorate. Making matters worse, locked wheels make directional control more difficult and make the aircraft vulnerable to crosswinds.

A landing starts 120 miles from the airport at 35,000 feet. Here is what pilots do between cruise and touchdown to set it up.

One of the main disadvantages of grooves is maintenance. Rubber from the aircraft tires accumulates in the grooves, especially at the touchdown zones. This can reduce their effectiveness over time. Consequently, grooves can add yet more maintenance for the airport. There are some other disadvantages of grooving beyond construction costs and maintenance, although they are typically manageable.

For instance, it can damage the pavement, add foreign object debris by accumulating rubber, slightly increase tire noise, and other minor considerations. One of the biggest cases against them is when the climate is dry. Wet airports like those in the US Pacific Northwest and Northern Europe can benefit from grooving. However, this does not transfer to dry airports, such as those in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, or Arizona.

With that being said, these areas can experience flash flooding, making grooving momentarily useful. At the same time, desert and sandy environments can increase the contamination problem, with grooves accumulating sand. A residual benefit is that in colder climates where there is ice and snow, grooves can retain anti-icing and de-icing chemicals. They can help drain melted snow and ice.

Modern airliners can lose traction on wet surfaces, but in cases where accidents have happened, hydroplaning is often seen as one contributing factor. Modern jets come with anti-skid braking, ground spoilers, thrust reversers, and autobrakes. Since 2000, one of the most notable incidents came in 2019, when a Boeing 737 operating as Miami Air International flight 293 overran the wet and ungrooved runway at Jacksonville.

The aircraft overran the runway into the St. Johns River, although there were no serious injuries. This accident happened at a US Navy airfield, not Jacksonville International Airport, and so was not covered under the 1997 FAA regulations. The NTSB report states that:

"The NTSB determined that the probable cause of the 2019 runway overrun of the Boeing 737 in Jacksonville, Florida, was, in part, 'an extreme loss of braking friction due to heavy rain and the water depth on the ungrooved runway, which resulted in viscous hydroplaning.'"

Another hydroplaning incident involved United Express in Ottawa in 2010, when an Embraer aircraft overran the wet and ungrooved runway. As previously noted, Ottawa became Canada's first airport with a grooved runway in 2013. Other notable incidents on this front included American Airlines flight 331 at Kingston (2009) and Southwest Airlines flight 1919 in Chicago (2011).

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Elsewhere, Virgin Australia suffered a similar occurrence on New Zealand's then-ungrooved Christchurch runway in 2015. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau found that Virgin Australia's company policy at the time treated damp runways as dry, leading to a miscalculation of landing performance requirements and high crew workload during a revised approach.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6161. Hegseth Impeachment Vote Imminent

There is a significant chance that one or more articles will be approved.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth testifies about the Pentagon’s fiscal year 2027 budget request before the House Armed Services Committee in Washington, D.C., April 29, 2026.

Eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have been proposed in the House by Representative Thomas Massie, a libertarian Republican from Kentucky who lost his seat when the president pushed for his ouster in a primary earlier this year. (The Trump-endorsed candidate, Ed Gallrein, retained the seat for the GOP last week despite the wave that will give Democrats solid majorities in both congressional chambers come January.)

Though still narrowly controlled by Republicans for the next two lame duck months, the House will be forced to consider Massie’s proposal. Impeachment is a privileged motion under House rules; action of some kind must be taken on it within two days after it is filed. Impeachments can stretch beyond a single session of Congress, so if the House impeaches Hegseth, a Senate trial could be postponed until January, when Democrats will have a commanding majority in the upper chamber.

#6160. Delta SkyMiles Gold Card Review: Solid Perks For Occasional Delta Flyers

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card is the mid-range personal credit card in the American Express and Delta co-brand card portfolio, which includes seven cards, covering a variety of annual fee levels, across both personal and business products.

This post is my in-depth review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Amex Card. The card has a reasonable annual fee and is ideal for someone looking for basic benefits that come in handy when flying Delta. However, if you’re a Medallion elite flyer on Delta, another card might be a better option (more on that below).

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card review, here’s a quick look at the card’s main selling points and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Delta Gold Amex welcome bonus and ongoing fees, since these are some of the most important features to consider when opening a new card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex is currently offering new cardholders the following bonus: You may be eligible for as high as 80,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $2,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $880.

This is a solid welcome bonus, though the card recently offered a higher one that included a statement credit along with bonus miles. Everyone has to decide for themselves whether they’d rather wait for a better offer, or apply with this offer so they can take advantage of the perks ASAP.

The welcome offer on the Delta Gold Amex card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past.

You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal versions of the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more) or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the Delta Gold Amex first. That’s because if you do, you’d potentially still be eligible for the Delta Platinum Amex and Delta Reserve Amex. Meanwhile if you apply for one of those cards first, you’d no longer be eligible for the “lesser” card.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score you need to get approved for the Delta Gold Amex. I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been denied, as it’s only one of many factors that determines card eligibility.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees). This is a great opportunity to try the card before you have to “buy” it. The card also has a reasonable annual fee on an ongoing basis, so it’s easy to recoup that fee by taking advantage of the card perks.

You can also add authorized users to the Delta Gold Amex at no extra cost.

If you are going to put spending on the card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees) with the Delta Gold Amex, so you can use the card abroad without paying those high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. Unfortunately the Delta Gold Amex isn’t much to get excited about on that front, but let’s still go over the details.

When it comes to the return on spending, the Delta Gold Card offers:

While it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling. There are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays it’s common to see airlines offer elite status qualification through credit card spending. Delta SkyMiles elite status is based on the concept of Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs), and it’s possible to earn elite status with credit card spending.

The catch is that the Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn any MQDs, so if you want to qualify for status, you’ll have to pick up the Delta Platinum Card or Delta Reserve Card. More on that later.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

As I’ll cover below, having the Delta Gold Amex also gives you access to the TakeOff 15 discount on award tickets, and that can also help you stretch your SkyMiles for travel on Delta.

The real reason you’ll want to keep the Delta Gold Card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which are great for the casual Delta flyer. Truthfully, this is the value proposition of many airline credit cards — it’s largely about the welcome bonus and the perks, so let’s take a closer look at those details for the Delta Gold Amex.

Perhaps one of the biggest incentives to actually spend money on the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is the ability to earn a flight credit. Specifically, if you spend $10,000 on the card in a calendar year, you can receive a $200 Delta eCredit to use toward future travel, which will be deposited right in your SkyMiles account. The credit expires one year after it’s issued.

Getting a $200 Delta eCredit in addition to any miles could be a good incentive to spend $10,000 on the card per year. The credit alone is the equivalent of a 2% return on spending, assuming you consider it to be worth face value.

Just for having the Delta Gold Card you receive up to $100 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $100 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $100, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex, you get a first checked bag free. You can also receive a second checked bag free on eligible domestic Delta flights.

This benefit is limited to the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for your flight with your Delta Amex, though you do need to have your SkyMiles number in the reservation.

With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up. A first checked bag on domestic flights costs $45, and a second costs $55, so even just checking one bag on two roundtrip flights could effectively cancel out the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Gold Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary card member’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation. This benefit is valid for the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation.

If you have the Delta Gold Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible inflight purchases of food and beverages. The statement credit will post within 8-12 weeks of an eligible purchase.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for 1.0 cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the Delta TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta flights booked through delta.com or the Fly Delta app. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card also comes with a rideshare credit. The way it works is that you get up to $10 back as a statement credits each month when you use the card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

You need to enroll in this benefit in order to get the money back, and it doesn’t kick in until after your first card renewal. So while it’s a useful perk if you already pay for rideshares at least once a month, it doesn’t really make or break the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in having as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. Note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card isn’t a card I’d be using for my everyday spending, since there are many more rewarding cards for that. However:

In other words, for someone who flies Delta occasionally, I think this card could make sense, and the benefits can more than offset the annual fee.

Meanwhile if you’re a more frequent Delta flyer, there could be value to having one of the more premium credit cards, which allow you to spend your way to elite status, and earn Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs).

If the Delta Gold Card sounds interesting to you, but you want a business card instead, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card. Learn more about applying for Amex business cards.

The Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (learn more) has a $0 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following benefits:

Beyond that, though, there are limited perks. If you’d get value out of a first checked bag free or priority boarding, then you’re much better off getting one of Delta’s cards with an annual fee. I can’t really see much upside to getting the Delta Blue Card, over the other options in the market.

The Delta Platinum Amex (learn more) has a higher annual fee of $350 (Rates & Fees) and offers more perks than the Delta Gold:

If you want to earn MQDs toward elite status and enjoy more Delta benefits, like an annual companion certificate, the Delta Platinum Amex is the better option between these two cards.

The Delta Reserve Card (learn more) is the most premium option among personal Delta Amex cards, with the highest annual fee: $650 (Rates & Fees)

It also has the most benefits, so it could be worth it if you frequently fly Delta and want the best perks like lounge access:

Those aren’t even all the Delta Reserve card benefits. It also lets you earn MQDs on spending and gets you upgrade priority over other Delta SkyMiles members with your same Medallion tier, product, and fare experience purchased. The annual fee is high, but it’s absolutely worth a look if you want as many Delta perks as possible.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers:

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is a card that can be worth holding onto for the benefits that it offers, like up to $100 in Delta Stays credit, free checked bags, priority boarding, inflight savings, and more.

For the more frequent Delta flyer, consider the Delta Platinum Card, which can offer a larger bonus and additional perks, but also has a higher annual fee. Meanwhile if you’re a true Delta frequent flyer, consider the Delta Reserve Card, which offers some lounge access perks, helps you qualify for status fastest, etc.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Gold Amex Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (Rates & Fees).

#6159. Alaska Airlines Launches Global Concierge—Its Answer To United Global Services And American ConciergeKey

Alaska Airlines has started inviting customers into Atmos Global Concierge, its new unpublished invitation-only top tier status along the lines of United Global Services, American Airlines ConciergeKey and Delta 360. The first reports point to an effort to win expensive international business class tickets, with benefits that include a next-flight guarantee during travel disruptions, dedicated assistance and Avis Chairman’s Club. Some of the early reaction has been that the benefits look underwhelming. I disagree. I used to have Avis Chairman’s Club, and it was special. And American’s next-flight guarantee came through for me when I needed it, having this benefit at Alaska could be really clutch. Invitations started surfacing November 9. One recipient shared this language: As one of our most valued status holders, you’ve been selected for two exceptional privileges: a complimentary upgrade to Atmos Titanium status and an inaugural membership in Atmos Global Concierge, our most elevated level of service. The invitation emphasizes travel across Europe, Asia and Oceania, backed by a dedicated team. Global Concierge membership begins immediately and runs through December 31, 2027. You’re invited to ATMOS GLOBAL CONCIERGE by u/iZoooom in AlaskaAirlines Alaska is giving these customers Titanium status and Global Concierge membership. What Atmos Global Concierge Members Get An invited member posted the following benefits in the discussion. Direct access to a concierge team. Proactive itinerary monitoring. A next-flight guarantee. Arrival assistance at destinations in Asia, Europe and Oceania. A car transfer at London Heathrow for tight connections. Upgrade priority on global flights. CLEAR+ membership. Avis Chairman’s Club. Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier. Who’s Getting Invited? There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. Avis Chairman’s Club May Be The Sleeper Benefit It’s easy to skim past rental car status in an airline benefits list. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full. Alaska Airlines has grown up, with premium international service and now a service tier for its top elite customers to match. An invited member posted the following benefits in the discussion. Direct access to a concierge team. Proactive itinerary monitoring. A next-flight guarantee. Arrival assistance at destinations in Asia, Europe and Oceania. A car transfer at London Heathrow for tight connections. Upgrade priority on global flights. CLEAR+ membership. Avis Chairman’s Club. Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier. Who’s Getting Invited? There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. Avis Chairman’s Club May Be The Sleeper Benefit It’s easy to skim past rental car status in an airline benefits list. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full. Alaska Airlines has grown up, with premium international service and now a service tier for its top elite customers to match. It’s worth reflecting on why this benefit is so valuable. Heathrow may have the best connections in the world but it has the worst connections between terminals. In 2026 there is no dedicated, all-terminal, airside connecting train. Shameful.

” and a valet ride back to the terminal.”

Throwing Concierge in there is most definitely a shot across the bow at their oneworld partner… wonder if they got permission first, or just went with it.

UA GLOBAL services AA CONCIERGEkey AS GLOBAL CONCIERGE

@1990 I’d suspect the opposite. It’s so strikingly familiar to Concierge Key that it seems like they’re actually trying to purposefully associate themselves with a different program but one that either airline elites will use..

Truly wild speculation on my part, but it does make one wonder if they could push for a joint mileage program as part of the rumored domestic JV. It would make a lot of sense if they did since there is some leakage and play between the two mileage programs for those that enjoy the game.

For the people underwhelmed by this, what do 360 and GS offer that this doesn’t? I’m legitimately asking, I’ll never get an invite like this

The real question is whether they can deliver. They have so many bungled processes, and staff that can’t even do a PDB half the time. I get that they’re trying to court high value flyers, but can they actually execute?

Interestingly no invite on my end. 173K status points mostly on international business, much of which is with partners, but also Alaska. I fly out of SFO though, which may have to do with it.

@ L3 — LHR terminal transfer isn’t so bad once you learn how it works. Just allow plenty of time and it’s not that bad.

I wonder if this will mostly be for west coast flyers, as they are most likely to fly international premium classes on AS?

So in the next flight is completely full I guess this means one of the poors, even with a guaranteed seat, gets bumped to make room for this elite traveler. And if the elite had a business class seat, some schmuck there gets bumped down to coach, with a coach passenger being knocked off the flight to make room.

Does Alaska have enough of a global network for this elite status to really make sense? Probably not for anyone who is not located in the Washington/Oregon area.

Many of the new flights don’t seem to have onward connecting opportunities. Does ICN? FCO? CDG? It’s really only in LHR and NRT. I don’t know to what extent AS has good connections and through fares. LHR really isn’t an efficient connecting hub. I prefer MUC, FRA, AMS – but AS doesn’t have partners.

I haven’t tried Alaska’s international service in part because they launched without Internet connectivity and the initial reviews were poor. Even today the Hawaiian crews get mixed reviews. I wonder if there has been enough time and enough trial for Alaska to be able to accurately identify who should qualify for the Global Concierge level. Maybe it will be primarily determined by their sales department seeking out corporate customers and giving it to top executives and travel executives. We shall see.

Alaska has historically been terrible at reaccommodating passengers during IRROPS. They don’t have adequate staff handling IRROPS and that staff isn’t supposed to rebook you onto other airlines if that’s the way to complete your journey. They usually limit themselves to their own metal and when they only serve a destination once a day, that can be a long wait. I guess that the Global Concierge level customers will be insulated from the poor IRROPs experience, especially if they relax the restrictions on rebooking onto OALs. Otherwise, the next available flight guarantee is of limited use if Alaska only flies once a day.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

When it comes to earning credit card rewards, sometimes two cards really are better than one.

Maybe you have a card that earns bonus points on dining and groceries but falls short on other everyday purchases. Or perhaps you love your card's travel perks but wish it offered better earning rates outside of travel.

That's where pairing cards can come in handy. By choosing two cards with complementary benefits and earning categories, you can get more out of your spending without relying on a single card for everything.

Here are three American Express card combinations worth considering, depending on your spending habits and travel goals.

Frequent travelers who want a combination of premium travel benefits and strong everyday earning rates may get the most value from pairing the with the .

The Platinum is, at its core, a travel and lifestyle card that offers access to an extensive network of airport lounges worldwide through the Global Lounge Collection, along with a range of statement credits and other travel benefits.

The Gold fills an important gap in the Platinum's earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $50,000 and $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, respectively*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

By using the Platinum for eligible flights and the Gold for dining and groceries, you can earn elevated rewards across several major spending categories while enjoying premium travel benefits. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can also combine your rewards into one balance to use toward travel through Amex's transfer partners (after linking your accounts online).

The trade-off of this card combination is cost. The Platinum has an $895 annual fee, while the Gold has a $325 annual fee, bringing the combined annual cost to $1,220. For that reason, I'd only recommend this pairing to travelers who can take advantage of the Platinum's benefits and who regularly spend in the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: How these two cards got me over $4,500 in value in one year

If you spend a lot on dining and groceries but want to earn more than 1 point per dollar spent on other eligible purchases, the and could make a great pair.

The Gold earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year*) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year*). It also earns 3 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through amextravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

Then, use the Blue Business Plus for eligible business purchases that would earn only 1 point per dollar on the Gold. It earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*) compared with the Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up a single rewards balance to use toward travel through Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Gold has a $325 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee, so you won't pay extra to add a flat-rate earning card to the mix.

Just keep in mind that the Blue Business Plus is a business card, so you'll need to qualify to apply. This combination could be especially useful for freelancers and small-business owners with eligible business expenses that don't fall into the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: The 4 Amex cards I’d use to earn Membership Rewards points faster

If your business spends a lot on things like advertising, software or gas, the and could make a great pair.

The Business Gold earns 4 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in combined purchases per calendar year*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

What I like about the Business Gold is that you don't have to choose your bonus categories in advance. Amex automatically determines your top two eligible categories each billing cycle, which is helpful if your business expenses change from month to month.

For purchases outside those categories, the Blue Business Plus earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*). That's double the Business Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

For example, you might use the Business Gold for advertising and software expenses, then switch to the Blue Business Plus for other eligible business purchases. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up one balance to use with Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Business Gold has a $375 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee. This combination makes the most sense if you spend enough in the Business Gold's bonus categories to justify the annual fee while using the Blue Business Plus to earn more on other purchases.

Related: 7 reasons why the Amex Blue Business Plus Card should be in everyone’s wallet

Before adding another Amex card to your wallet, take a look at where you're spending the most money and what you want to get out of your rewards. The goal is to find a card that fills a gap in your current lineup, rather than one that offers more of the same.

And remember, earning more points isn't worth it if you're spending more than you normally would or carrying a balance and paying interest.

Related: Best credit card strategies for couples

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to choosing the best credit card combination. The key is finding cards that complement each other rather than simply offer more of the same benefits.

Whether you're looking for premium travel perks, stronger everyday earning rates or a way to maximize rewards on business expenses, pairing the right Amex cards can help you earn more Membership Rewards points.

Just make sure the additional rewards and benefits are worth the combined annual fees and that you're choosing cards that make sense for your spending habits.

Related: The best business and personal credit card combinations

#6157. British Airways Unveils 7 New International Routes: See Full List Now

British Airways has disclosed five new or returning routes. Not only are they from London Heathrow and London City, but also from Edinburgh and Glasgow. BA mainline and BA CityFlyer will operate them.

Other routes have already been revealed for 2027. BA will relaunch flights from Heathrow to Melbourne, this time via Kuala Lumpur rather than Singapore, while beginning service from London Gatwick to Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar.

On April 15, BA will take off from Heathrow to Bergen. Not only does Bergen have the second most populous metro population in Norway, but it is also a significant tourist destination for the highly beautiful fjords and cruises. BA will fly five times weekly, mainly on the Airbus A319. The lack of consistency in the following schedule is, of course, primarily due to LHR's renowned slot shortage.

This is not a new route for BA. OAG shows that the oneworld member previously flew from Heathrow to Bergen between 2012 and 2017, with up to two daily flights. BA had inherited the short route from bmi, which had served it from early 2011. BA will be one of only two operators from London to the Scandinavian city next year, joining Norwegian to Gatwick.

Then there's the Greek tourist destination of Skiathos, which is reasonably well-known for the very low final approach over a road. It is the St. Maarten of Europe. Covering 1,245 nautical miles (2,306 km), BA will operate three times weekly using the A320neo from May 20. It'll replace London City-Skiathos, which BA CityFlyer has served since 2017.

Significantly, it'll be the first time that the UK's busiest airport has had flights to Skiathos. While subject to change and reflecting the extent of higher-end premium leisure travel, Heathrow will now have nonstop flights to 12 destinations in Greece. Only Gatwick and Stansted will have a more extensive network (16 destinations).

All the following additions involve BA CityFlyer, whose fleet consists entirely of the 106-seat Embraer E190 due to its London City operations. On May 1, the regional jet unit will take off from London City to Perugia, with a weekly operation.

It'll replace Heathrow-Perugia flights, which have operated since 2022. This will be the first time the Italian destination has been served from LCY. The 'downtown' London airport will now have flights to four cities in Italy.

On May 15, BA CityFlyer will introduce a weekly service from Edinburgh to Split and Glasgow to Nice. Using aircraft that would otherwise be grounded for half the weekend due to London City's closure, the BA unit is used to flying from airports across the UK on weekends, especially during the summer. However, it appears that summer activity from Stansted has been axed next year.

One of the airlines has cut more routes than the other two carriers combined. Find out which here!

Reflecting what is known as of November 11, BA will introduce the following routes in 2027. Flights from Heathrow to Melbourne will resume after a 20-year absence. Significantly, BA will follow the launch of fellow oneworld member Finnair, which debuted in Melbourne at the end of October 2026.

One of the most notable developments is BA's return to Tanzania. The airline last flew there in 2013, when it served Dar es Salaam, which is the largest city but not the capital. Things will be very different in 2027, when BA will fly to tourist-driven Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar. The operating Triple Seven will fly Gatwick-Kilimanjaro-Zanzibar-Gatwick. You can read more about the new offering here.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6156. ATMA: Aman’s New Brand, Debuting With A 1,049-Foot Miami Tower

Aman is known for being one of the world’s top luxury hotel groups. Currently Aman Group consists of Aman (the original hotel group) and Janu (intended to be more of a “lifestyle” version of Aman). Aman is now launching a third brand, and it’s yet another departure from the origins of Aman.

Aman Group has announced the launch of ATMA, described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” ATMA means “the spirit” or “the true self” in Sanskrit, and the intent is for the brand to combine wellness, sport, nutrition-led dining, design, and experiential entertainment.

ATMA will “focus on advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities, which have been developed exclusively by ATMA Global Partner Novak Djokovic.”

The first location will be ATMA Miami, and it will include a hotel, branded residence, and a private members club. Specifically, the property will be in the Brickell neighborhood and will have a private marina, with an anticipated opening in 2031.

ATMA Miami is expected to be a standalone 1,049-foot tower, which is as tall as buildings can get in Miami. In terms of height, it’ll be match the new 100-story Waldorf Astoria Miami that’s currently under construction, which will be the tallest building in Florida, once complete.

Details about ATMA Miami are still fairly limited, but we know there will be 480 residential units, in addition to the hotel. Residential units will be between one and six bedrooms, and will be “supported by Aman Group’s service standards.”

There will also be a 120,000 square foot spa and wellness area, set to be the largest of its kind in Miami. Developed in partnership with Djokovic, it will offer performance and recovery experiences alongside indoor padel, tennis and squash courts, a fitness center, group and private training studios, mobility and conditioning labs, a medical wellness center, and dedicated recovery spaces.

So far we’ve only learned about the Miami location, but the claim is that the brand will span urban and remote destinations.

Look, I’ve made my opinions about the Aman brand pretty clear, so I don’t want to sound like some old dude just ranting about the “good old days.” When Aman was founded by hospitality legend Adrian Zecha, it was truly among the most innovative and passion driven hospitality projects we’ve ever seen.

In 2014, Zecha sold the brand to Vladislav Doronin, and since then, the entire philosophy has changed. It’s hard to fault someone for purchasing a brand and trying to cash in and maximize profitability — I mean, that’s kind of how the business world is supposed to work, right?

But of course that doesn’t mean we have to be happy about the evolution. It started with Aman ditching its approach of largely opening hotels in the middle of nowhere, where that was part of the charm. Instead, we saw Aman focus on city hotels. Then Aman became all about opening members clubs. Then we saw the launch of the Janu brand, essentially a higher room count version of Aman, with a more lively spirit.

And now we’re seeing Aman getting into building full-on skyscrapers. Well, or at least partnering on them in terms of branding. Of course some Aman properties already have a residences component, so that’s nothing new, as such. However, the scale of this project couldn’t be more opposite of what Aman initially was. We’re talking about a 100-story building that will have nearly 500 residences, and who knows how many hotel rooms (it hasn’t yet been announced).

Of course in Miami, one of the biggest trends is branded residences, with brands just selling out their name. But if Aman were to just slap its name on a residential project, you’d think it would be something smaller scale than this. This is among the highest unit count developments we’ve ever seen in Miami, at least for a project spanning just one building.

Aman Group has just announced its third brand, and it will be named ATMA. It’s described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” The first location will open in Miami in 2031, and it’ll be a roughly 100-story building with 480 residences, a hotel, and a members club.

Aman as a brand has become unrecognizable compared to what it was 15 years ago. But that’s fair enough, and it’s also what happens when you sell a company to someone looking to maximize their ROI. You can hardly fault someone for that, as much as I don’t personally like it.

I like the concept of someone creating a modern, wellness-focused luxury brand where all the food is organic / not ultraprocessed, products don’t contain chemicals, etc. Six Senses has totally lost its way under IHG and there really isn’t anyone else. I don’t think opening first in the filler / anti-vax capital of the world signals this is it, though.

I’m curious how these rich people shoeboxes work out for the developers given the collapsing SoFlo real estate market. Is the top end still selling? They can’t survive on the high-end hotels in those developments alone. And while rich people tend to be a bit oblivious to reality, how appealing really is holding a property on sargassum overwhelmed beaches and cities where sewage runs through the streets with each flooding? But I’m sure the restaurant, oh so lovely, and the pool ..

Tell me a brand that has not done this? Four Seasons, only. Period. Aman can learn a lot from staying true to the core of their vision like Four Seasons. But they won't. It's being run now by investors who envision something far bigger and hitting every demographic. Which is the Bonvoy model. Probably not long before they become part of Bonvoy. I'm joking, I think? In many ways it is similar to fashion brands. Years of being indie and true to its purpose. Only to be gobbled up and expanded to reach different markets. Cucinelli is the last of them today. Like Four Seasons with hotels. They will all fall eventually. And with so much controlled by the few it will be impossible for innovators, like Aman once was, to ever create new ideas. Our existence will become visiting factories of "experience" that are stale and boring. Obnoxious even. I say get a tent. And find a mountain. And there build your own Aman experience for a week.

There's nothing wrong with a brand evolving and pivoting into something new and unfound. Clearly new ownership thought higher room counts would maximize margins. If the people don't like it, they can vote with their dollars. It's not like Brickell is short of places to stay/live.

#6155. The Don Jr. Wedding May Be the Emblem of a Corrupt Age

‘Hogs get slaughtered,’ as the old saying goes — people will tolerate graft only up to a point.

Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, disembark from Air Force One at Dublin Airport in Dublin, Ireland, September 12, 2026.

On May 31, 1871, William Marcy Tweed threw a spectacularly lavish wedding for his daughter, Mary Amelia, in New York City. “Boss” Tweed was then at the height of his power as the political master of New York City, its ruling Democratic Party, and its Tammany Hall machine. Elected to the U.S. House at 29 in 1852, he sacrificed his career in Washington to vote for the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which was massively unpopular in the North. This was not a stance on principle: The vote was a test of party loyalty, and the Pierce administration paid off Tweed by appointing a friend to a job as postmaster. Returning home to New York, Tweed was running Tammany Hall by 1858.

The corruption he oversaw was immense. It at least doubled the cost of building anything that the city could touch. The Tweed Courthouse cost some $13-14 million to build, twice the cost of the Alaska Purchase during the same period. David McCullough argued in The Great Bridge that the Brooklyn Bridge would never have been completed had the Tweed Ring not fallen early in its construction. Tweed and his cronies were convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars — some modern estimates place the real amount in the hundreds of millions — which would be worth billions today. Alfred Ely Beach, who published Scientific American, decided to build a pioneering subway line between 1868 and 1870, powered by an immense pneumatic tube, and to avoid paying off Tweed, he built it like a bank heist, removing the dirt at night and not telling the city what he was building until it was ready for passengers.

Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

#6154. Will Credit Card Interest Rates Be Capped At 10%? Democrats Want To Work With Trump

With the recent midterm elections, the balance of power in Washington is very quickly changing. Given the extent to which things shifted left, Democrats certainly want to be able to show that they can accomplish something in the next two years, to make life better for average Americans.

Along those lines, we’re once again seeing a proposal floated regarding capping credit card interest rates. There’s a lot more support for this than in the past, given the majority that Democrats have, plus the fact that President Trump has also been in support of this concept (or at least claimed to be). Will it actually pass, though?

Senate Democrats are renewing a proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, with Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts specifically bringing this up in a “Face The Nation” interview. Warren is likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee, and could use her position to help advance the proposal.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president. “We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price… pic.twitter.com/0r17PwXPQT

Now, before anyone gets political, keep in mind that this is a concept that Trump actually proposed earlier this year. He claimed that Americans were being ripped off by credit card companies, and that as of January 20, 2026, credit card interest rates should be capped at 10%. However, this just came in the form of a social media post, rather than any actual legislation:

Please be informed that we will no longer let the American Public be “ripped off” by Credit Card Companies that are charging Interest Rates of 20 to 30%, and even more, which festered unimpeded during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration. AFFORDABILITY! Effective January 20, 2026, I, as President of the United States, am calling for a one year cap on Credit Card Interest Rates of 10%. Coincidentally, the January 20th date will coincide with the one year anniversary of the historic and very successful Trump Administration. Thank you for your attention to this matter. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP

Donald J. Trump Truth Social Post 08:10 PM EST 01.09.26 pic.twitter.com/47SQ03yMeo

Unsurprisingly, there was no enforcement mechanism, and this never happened, especially since he got pushback from other Republicans. If he really believed in that proposal, then it sounds like this will be his chance to actually turn it into some sort of a law, with support from Democrats. We’ll have to mark this as “developing” for now.

Just for some context, credit card issuers make money in three primary ways — through interchange fees, through interest charges, and through annual fees. When it comes to interest rates, credit card companies are known for having very high rates, an average of over 20%. These are the charges that apply if you don’t pay your full balance before the payment due date. You don’t pay interest charges if you simply charge your purchase to a credit card, and then pay your balance in full.

On the surface, capping credit card interest rates of course sounds great — some of the rates are really high, and many people view banks as greedy, and think they can afford to give up some of their margins. Obviously for those who are currently financing charges, a cap on interest rates would be positive.

The thing is, a policy change like this wouldn’t come without some other changes. There’s no denying that if interest rates were capped at 10%, lots of consumers with not-great credit would be locked out of getting credit cards, and might even have their accounts closed, because card issuers would find it too risky to loan them money at that rate.

After all, there’s a huge risk to people not making payments, and the economics of that work differently with 10% interest rates rather than 25% interest rates. I would imagine that tens of millions of Americans would have their accounts closed, that we’d see fewer no annual fee cards, etc.

Beyond that, if we did see a long term cap on credit card interest rates, it would likely change the credit card landscape in terms of how rewarding cards are, with everything ranging from welcome bonuses, to rewards on spending, to perks.

Right or wrong, credit card economics are heavily reliant on a cross-subsidized system. That’s the whole reason some of us are able to get such outsized value. Credit card rewards structures nowadays largely more or less rebate back interchange fees to consumers, as it’s easy to earn 2% cash back with cards, or even to earn huge multipliers on spending.

The reality is that the revenue that subsidizes a lot of rewards is the interest charges, since that’s the highest margin revenue stream from many card issuers. So we’re partly earning huge welcome bonuses and 5x points on some transactions because someone else is paying close to 30% interest.

I’m not saying that’s a good system, but I’m just being realistic about how it works. If interest rates are forced to be slashed by more than half in the long run, it will have major implications for rewards. Maybe that’s objectively not a bad thing, but it will happen.

For that matter, it would even have a major impact on airlines — they’re so reliant on credit card revenue nowadays to turn profits, and this would greatly hurt their margins in that area as well.

With Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, there’s a renewed push to cap credit card interest rates at 10%. This is a proposal that Trump made earlier this year, but it didn’t get support from Republicans.

While I totally appreciate that credit card interest rates are often incredibly high, it’s not without reason, given the rate of default on some cards. Approval standards for cards would change, many consumers would have their cards shut down, etc. It would also likely change the economics of the credit card industry, which could even impact airlines.

However, I’m not some lobbyist or apologist for the credit card industry. If the change happens, many people will benefit, and I’m sure the industry will adapt. However, unarguably many people will go from paying 25% interest on their credit card, to potentially paying even higher rates for payday loans, doing business with loan sharks, etc.

What do you make of this proposal to cap credit card interest rates?

There are many ways to deal with this, but capping rates at 10% won't happen; it would destroy the entire business model. Lots and I mean lots of people would see their cards cancelled or their credit limits lowered, resulting in many people having to repay funds and look elsewhere for credit. Ripple effect on the economy, etc. In Quebec, they raised the legal minimum payment you have to make on credit cards from next to nothing to 5%. The Bank of Canada had a detailed report on credit cards in Canada, and the summary was that access to credit was diminished, and delinquency rates went up slightly, but people carried less debt on average. Nothing earth-shattering, but I guess it's a positive change if people have less debt. I think people should be better educated that credit cards should not be used as a loan. You should never spend money you don't have except for a mortgage. I know that's not easy when you are young.

following short term rates & set monthly by fed, prime + 10% seems a solid compromise. currently prime is 7% so 17% cc interest rate cap. a haircut on our rewards ecosystem seems likely if a law emerges. deal with it!

Within the public debt markets, there are credit rating agencies that assign AAA, AA+, AA, AA-, A+, etc. Each rating has a historic average default rate and an interest rate premium consistent with that default rate. It would seem consistent and reasonable to tie an individual's interest rate to that person's credit score.

Honestly, I think the incoming Congress might very well pass a 10% interest rate limit. The question would then be will Trump veto it? If that happens, even though Democrats made huge gains in the recent elections, it likely will not be law as they won't have anything approaching a veto-proof majority in either house. @Ben, I agree with your analysis. Current credit card interest rates are legalized usury but if restricted, we can kiss a lot of related loyalty program perks good-bye. I am starting to see another trend that will affect credit card usage: pushback from merchants, who are tacking on fees for using credit cards. If this trend continues, it will cost you more to get those points and miles. Some merchants who tack on credit card usage fees don't do that for debit cards. Apparently, the fees they pay banks for debit card usage are lower than for credit cards. However, in the US, there is a legal liability limit of $50 per fraudulent credit card transaction. That limit does NOT apply to fraudulent debit card transactions, making debit card usage relatively dangerous in this day and age, as it exposes your entire bank balance to fraud. Debit card transactions should probably also be protected against fraud but if that happened, banks would likely just raise merchant fees to match credit card fees or maybe even higher fee levels as the loss potential is higher.

Maybe there will be a carve out for cards with benefits (travel, hotel, airline, etc) to a different higher cap

#6153. New Bilt Deals With Hyatt, Marriott And Sports Team Reveal Bigger Bet On Rewards Across Your Whole Neighborhood

Bilt wants the building you live in, the hotel program you belong to, and the team you root for to get you recognized and rewarded at businesses around you. Its new Neighborhood OS and membership platform bring together merchants, housing communities, Hyatt, Marriott and professional sports teams in a much bigger play than earning points on rent. The ambition is to become the company that helps businesses find their next customer, gives that customer a reason to do business, and makes the experience good enough that they come back. I’ve been writing about Bilt’s distribution advantage since 2021. They figured out how to reach customers everyone else wanted but failed to reach – through their homes. They’ve since built what I consider the most valuable points currency and the best rewards for my everyday credit card spending. Now they’re opening up the technology and merchant network behind those rewards for other companies to use. There are two pieces to the announcement: Tools for merchants. Neighborhood OS connects the reservation, payment, point of sale and loyalty systems a business already uses. The goal is to help it recognize customers, deliver benefits, bring in new business and encourage repeat visits. Loyalty programs for other organizations. Bilt is making its membership platform available under other companies’ brands. A sports team, hotel company or residential community can build a new membership program, or extend its existing one, with benefits at businesses around it. The partners include the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings; Marriott and Hyatt; and real estate companies including Related and Presidio Bay. Broader integrations and new membership experiences will roll out in phases beginning in 2027. Bilt CEO Ankur Jain describes a $6.6 trillion opportunity in annual U.S. retail and food services spending that takes place in person. That’s the size of the market they’re aiming at. Small goals! “Your neighborhood is your most important amenity.” — Ankur Jain, introducing Bilt Neighborhood OS What originally interested me in Bilt was the way they acquired customers. An airline already has people who want its miles sitting on its planes. A new, independent rewards program has to find consumers, persuade them to join, and give them a reason to stick around. That’s tough, but Bilt had a truly original angle in reaching people through their homes, rewarding them for paying rent. Bilt helped solve billing and resident relationship problems for landlords, and found a way to become focal for customers. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is an especially valuable moment: someone is choosing a new coffee shop, gym, dry cleaner and place to order dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. The company says it has signed one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. Their customers are far broader than the small minority of Bilt members with one of their credit cards. They’re equally happy for you to participate with whatever cards you already carry. We’ve seen attempts to create a common rewards program across different merchants before. American Express launched Plenti in 2015 with companies including AT&T, ExxonMobil, Macy’s and Rite Aid. It shut down in July 2018. Bilt’s chairman Ken Chenault was running American Express when Plenti launched. Plenti had enormous merchants with plenty of customers, but struggled to create was a compelling new relationship that made those customers change where they spent. The tech wasn’t very good, they didn’t broaden out merchants, and the value proposition was more modest. Coalition programs have a much longer history abroad. Canada’s Air Miles built a huge membership, although its financial troubles led to BMO acquiring it in 2023. Britain’s Nectar has 24 million active users. The U.S. still hasn’t produced a modern coalition on the scale Plenti promised. Bilt, though, offers a better way to reach customers and a more leveraged rewards system. A small discount is worth its face value. Points that can become a great hotel stay or an international business class award can be worth a lot more to the member than they cost to deliver. And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g. a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert). And their scale gives local merchants a much more compelling rewards program than they could have on their own. A customer might never visit one restaurant often enough to care about its standalone program. But their rewards can pool with others in the community to create something customers value. And they can reach the customers of those other local businesses, too. That restaurant can identify someone as a customer to solicit and a potentially valuable client to treat especially well. So for merchants: Find customers who can become regulars. A restaurant with empty tables on Tuesday can reach people in nearby buildings who are deciding where to eat. Spend the reward budget where it helps. An offer can be aimed at a first visit, a quiet evening or someone who hasn’t returned recently without giving away half the bill to everyone on a Saturday night when the restaurant is already full. Connect the visit to the relationship. Reservations, purchases and loyalty information can help the business recognize a customer, remember preferences and follow up. A good owner does this for the regulars they know, but the software can help scale it for more people. Offer something customers value more than it costs. A complimentary appetizer, a preferred table when available, or access to an otherwise empty fitness class can make a customer feel appreciated without requiring an equivalent cash discount. There’s a second distribution advantage here. Bilt is working with Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable. Those companies already have relationships with merchants and systems inside their businesses. Connecting to that installed base makes expansion much easier than persuading every restaurant to replace its payment terminal and reservation software. Bilt’s tech is better than what others have tried in the past. Here’s Bilt’s illustration of the merchant experience: The artificial intelligence component isn’t just buzz marketing. They can handle requests and coordinate actions across systems that otherwise require staff to do the work manually. Being able to identify the audience, make an offer, apply it correctly and help the merchant understand what happened is more useful. And Bilt says 91% of actions are completed without manual intervention. I’m not sure if that’s really good, or if a 9% failure rate is unacceptably high at scale. But it’ll clearly improve quickly. Bilt’s merchant sales page lists a $495 monthly Neighborhood OS subscription and an optional $195 monthly Neighborhood Marketplace subscription, or $690 for both. It lists a $1,500 onboarding fee waived through December 31, 2026. Bilt says members generated more than $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local merchants over the last year. A hotel company has a relationship with a guest while they’re traveling, but the guest spends money at restaurants and shops outside the hotel. A sports team has fans all year, including days when there’s no game. Those are valuable relationships with plenty of spending happening outside the company’s own business. Sports fans. The Phoenix Suns and Phoenix Mercury plan to launch in spring 2027 inside their existing app including concession offers, the ability to purchase seat upgrades when inventory opens, and neighborhood benefits connected to team wins. A fan concierge could help with a ride after the game or a restaurant offer nearby. Hotel loyalty. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. Marriott is also named as a partner. Delivery and dining. Grubhub’s partnership is designed to connect delivery and restaurant visits. A restaurant could encourage someone who orders at home to come in for dinner, or give a diner a reason to order delivery later, through connected campaigns. Bilt announced a $300 million acquisition of LAVA last week, bringing relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 technology adapters. That buys both access to fan communities and connections to the systems those teams use. Bilt calls its consumer pass Neighborhood Pass and has an identity system that lets businesses recognize eligible customers across systems without exchanging raw customer data. Getting the benefit applied correctly is a big part of the value. Nobody wants to explain a promotion to a waiter who’s never heard of it. In contrast, one senior executive who sought my counsel on whether to work with Plenti a decade ago concluded it was a non-starter that customers were going to have to submit individual receipts to the program for credit. I already get value from Bilt that goes well beyond a points balance. I’ve redeemed Bilt Cash this year for two BLADE flights, Blacklane and hotel discounts, and use benefits with Lyft, Grubhub and Walgreens. The opportunity here is to make useful benefits available across many more of the places people already spend time. Bilt already earns merchant commissions for sending spending to partners. Subscription fees add another revenue stream. Aggregating many small businesses gives it something valuable to offer a national hotel company, bank or sports sponsor. Bringing those companies’ customers and budgets to local merchants makes joining more attractive. They raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025. That provides resources to build and buy the technology, sign partners and support expansion. I think they have a real shot, but what they are doing is really hard. But each piece they successfully build makes subsequent pieces more valuable. A restaurant makes the network more useful to residents nearby. Those residents make it more attractive to the next merchant. A competitor has to assemble both sides in the same places. Two sided markets are hard! Bilt, which launched publicly just five years ago, has built this incredibly quickly.
