A hotel company has a relationship with a guest while they’re traveling, but the guest spends money at restaurants and shops outside the hotel. A sports team has fans all year, including days when there’s no game. Those are valuable relationships with plenty of spending happening outside the company’s own business.

Hotel loyalty. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. Marriott is also named as a partner.

Delivery and dining. Grubhub’s partnership is designed to connect delivery and restaurant visits. A restaurant could encourage someone who orders at home to come in for dinner, or give a diner a reason to order delivery later, through connected campaigns.

Bilt announced a $300 million acquisition of LAVA last week, bringing relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 technology adapters. That buys both access to fan communities and connections to the systems those teams use.

Bilt calls its consumer pass Neighborhood Pass and has an identity system that lets businesses recognize eligible customers across systems without exchanging raw customer data. Getting the benefit applied correctly is a big part of the value. Nobody wants to explain a promotion to a waiter who’s never heard of it. In contrast, one senior executive who sought my counsel on whether to work with Plenti a decade ago concluded it was a non-starter that customers were going to have to submit individual receipts to the program for credit.

I already get value from Bilt that goes well beyond a points balance. I’ve redeemed Bilt Cash this year for two BLADE flights, Blacklane and hotel discounts, and use benefits with Lyft, Grubhub and Walgreens. The opportunity here is to make useful benefits available across many more of the places people already spend time.

Bilt already earns merchant commissions for sending spending to partners. Subscription fees add another revenue stream. Aggregating many small businesses gives it something valuable to offer a national hotel company, bank or sports sponsor. Bringing those companies’ customers and budgets to local merchants makes joining more attractive.

They raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025. That provides resources to build and buy the technology, sign partners and support expansion. I think they have a real shot, but what they are doing is really hard. But each piece they successfully build makes subsequent pieces more valuable. A restaurant makes the network more useful to residents nearby. Those residents make it more attractive to the next merchant. A competitor has to assemble both sides in the same places. Two sided markets are hard! Bilt, which launched publicly just five years ago, has built this incredibly quickly. This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

They want to be a middleman and they’ve done payment processing for some big landlords. Exciting. Unfortunately, their 2026 was a complete disaster – dumped by a real bank, picked up by PE who wanted pie in the sky but instead got 3 versions of a credit card in 8 months that never achieved any market penetration. On the heels of that failure they’re pulling the rug out from the only part of the credit card that offered a bit more value to consumers than they could get from reliable banks.

All that means is that the marketing dollars they put into their growth plan did not result in more growth, so the marketing dollars had to be cut off because the hockey stick growth that would have supported the charade never materialized.

Now, of course, they have PE investors that would like to make some money off of this failure. So what do they do? They have some digital infrastructure that is underutilized and that they’d like to more broadly deploy. So back to basics… meaningless puffery and branding! They’re trying to refocus on the “meh” stuff that they originally did, because when pie in the sky fails, that’s what you do. Notably absent from this announcement though are any real, meaningful partnerships for “the Neighborhood OS”. Such branding and hubris.

Anyway, good news everyone, our neighborhoods are about to be brought together like never before by Bilt’s amazing AI capabilities… you know, the ones that couldn’t even answer questions about its own program accurately? In fairness, Bilt executives couldn’t answer questions about its own program accurately, so seems harsh to blame the AI.

Enjoy the grandfathering while it lasts, folks.

Wuttt. This was supposed to be a big jetBlue announcement day. So much for that… Oof. So, they’re now pulling an Allbirds, Boom Supersonic “but, but, actually, we’re now an AI company”? Very 2024/2025 of them. I think they missed the gravy train on that one.

This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

Re Sports teams sponsorships, hopefully they only view it as an advertising for new customers /sponsorship sort of thing. I have no interest in redeeming my points for watching overpriced US franchises.

@Too many – I think Bilt has been talking about that exactly

Remember, all of this is only worth $620, less than most other cards. Frequent Miler says so, and thye are so omniscient they don’t even need facts to prove it.

At the end of the day, loyalty programs operate within the razor-thin margins of retail. Why would these businesses fund rewards for another ecosystem instead of their own?

No amount of corporate spin can hide the obvious: Bilt bought market share with a credit card point system they certainly lost money on. Pretending it’s business genius to attract cardholders when you literally paid for them to be your customer is a choice.

“And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g., a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert).”

I love this fairy tale of “integrated rewards” where one credit seamlessly leads to another in a virtuous cycle. That is completely disconnected from how consumers actually behave. Nobody plans a night out three months in advance around stringing together a free Lyft, a free appetizer, and an ice cream.

People burn rewards when they get them or hoard them for flight. Marketers love drawing neat, circular diagrams of loyalty ecosystems, but real usage is jagged.

And sports? Live entertainment and sports are notorious for offering terrible value. At this point, it’s literally cheaper to take my girlfriend to Italy than it is to buy a decent seat at MSG against a competitor.

Hotel Loyalty? Once everyone is special, no one is.

And Grubhub? It’s the bottom of the barrel among delivery platforms. Every single party in the food delivery economy is miserable: consumers get gouged by markups and fees, drivers make pennies, and restaurants watch their margins get stripped away.

Want a real loyalty program? Become a regular at your local neighborhood spot. Get to know the owner, the bartenders, and the staff. You’ll get far more genuine hospitality, comped drinks, and a sense of community by supporting a local business than you ever will churning points.

#6151. United Airlines Pilot Couldn’t Fly After A Stroke—His Union Urged Removal, And His Military Bias Suit Failed

A United Airlines pilot left for military duty in September 2001, planning to come back two years later. Instead, he was furloughed, suffered a stroke, lost his medical clearance and eventually learned that his own union had recommended removing him from the airline’s seniority list. Twenty-five years after that leave began, William Michael Bumpus has lost his military discrimination lawsuit. On November 6, a federal judge in Chicago ruled that he hadn’t produced evidence that his military service motivated United’s decisions. United hired Bumpus in June 2000 and assigned him to Denver. He took approved leave in September 2001 to serve with the Air Force Reserve’s 706th Fighter Squadron, expecting to return in September 2003. Then United furloughed him in 2002, along with many other pilots. The airline struggled after 9/11 and went through a prolonged bankruptcy. According to his amended complaint, he was at Barksdale Air Force Base when a United supervisor called. He explained that he’d stay employed by the Air Force. On September 5, 2006, Bumpus suffered a stroke while on active duty. He was hospitalized and lost the medical certification he needed to fly. The record establishes that this happened during military service, but there’s no indication military service caused the stroke. United recalled him in May 2007. He accepted and told the airline about his medical condition. He didn’t request leave, although the recall offered that option. In January 2008, United told him he’d remain furloughed, with his recall rights expiring in March 2012 if he didn’t obtain medical clearance. He couldn’t fly for United, but the airline was still holding his space open. His employee record showed United returning him to active status and furloughing him again on March 2, 2009. A new furlough could start a fresh ten-year recall period, extending his right to return until March 2019. United offered another recall in 2012, and he requested a military deferment, which the airline acknowledged. His military service ended in March 2013. He still lacked medical clearance and bypassed another recall that September. In 2015, United’s furlough return coordinator told him he’d looked further into the case and confirmed the March 2019 deadline. Then, in 2017, the Air Line Pilots Association reviewed irregularities in United’s seniority list. The union recommended removing Bumpus. United agreed, concluding that his recall rights had expired in 2012. In January 2019, Bumpus sought to return and obtain medical leave to preserve his employment while resolving his medical certification. United initially told him his recall rights ran until March 2019. Days later, the airline reversed itself: its review with the union showed those rights had already expired. He finally obtained a first class medical certificate in June 2020, nearly fourteen years after the stroke. United had offered to consider him as a new hire, but he didn’t apply. He wanted his original seniority. Bumpus pursued a grievance and, in 2021, sued United and the union to obtain access to arbitration. The union wouldn’t take his case forward. He eventually got an arbitration hearing, but his grievance was dismissed as untimely in March 2023. He filed a lawsuit in June 2023, seeking reinstatement with full seniority, lost pay and other damages. He alleged that United accommodated other pilots and brought back 111 pilots without military service while refusing to restore him. His claims under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act took two different approaches: United owed him reemployment after military service. This included his argument that it should accommodate his medical condition through leave or an appropriate alternative position. United treated him worse because of his military service. He pointed to other pilots who received leave or returned with their seniority intact. I’ve covered an American Airlines case involving a reservist who couldn’t legally fly but was nevertheless entitled to prompt reemployment in an appropriate role. But Bumpus lost his reemployment claims in May 2025. The judge found that his absence from September 2001 to his accepted recall in May 2007 exceeded the law’s five-year service limit. He argued that time spent on economic furlough shouldn’t count: United wasn’t offering him work during those years anyway. What remained was discrimination. Bumpus needed evidence that his military service was at least one reason for United’s actions. His argument about leave ran into a basic problem: he hadn’t requested it in 2007. He also hadn’t shown that the other pilots received leave without asking. United’s treatment of those pilots didn’t establish that it denied him the same benefit because he served in the military. He did seek medical accommodation in 2019. By then, however, United and the union believed his recall rights had expired. The judge assumed, for purposes of deciding the case, that Bumpus was right about the 2019 deadline. Even with that assumption, he hadn’t shown military bias. United also removed two pilots with no military background after concluding their recall rights had expired, too. So even if United miscalculated, it wasn’t motivated by anti-military bias. The pilot here wasn’t punished for his service. He couldn’t fly for United for years and they held out a spot for him anyway. It’s a complicated case that generated contradictory answers about exactly what his rights were under a union contract and government requirements. The union agreed he should lose his seniority. His medical clearance eventually expired again in 2024. He last flew for United a quarter century ago, and he can’t currently fly even if he wanted to. Twenty-five years after that leave began, William Michael Bumpus has lost his military discrimination lawsuit. On November 6, a federal judge in Chicago ruled that he hadn’t produced evidence that his military service motivated United’s decisions.

United hired Bumpus in June 2000 and assigned him to Denver. He took approved leave in September 2001 to serve with the Air Force Reserve’s 706th Fighter Squadron, expecting to return in September 2003.

Then United furloughed him in 2002, along with many other pilots. The airline struggled after 9/11 and went through a prolonged bankruptcy. According to his amended complaint, he was at Barksdale Air Force Base when a United supervisor called. He explained that he’d stay employed by the Air Force.

On September 5, 2006, Bumpus suffered a stroke while on active duty. He was hospitalized and lost the medical certification he needed to fly. The record establishes that this happened during military service, but there’s no indication military service caused the stroke.

United recalled him in May 2007. He accepted and told the airline about his medical condition. He didn’t request leave, although the recall offered that option. In January 2008, United told him he’d remain furloughed, with his recall rights expiring in March 2012 if he didn’t obtain medical clearance. He couldn’t fly for United, but the airline was still holding his space open.

His employee record showed United returning him to active status and furloughing him again on March 2, 2009. A new furlough could start a fresh ten-year recall period, extending his right to return until March 2019.

United offered another recall in 2012, and he requested a military deferment, which the airline acknowledged. His military service ended in March 2013. He still lacked medical clearance and bypassed another recall that September.

In 2015, United’s furlough return coordinator told him he’d looked further into the case and confirmed the March 2019 deadline.

Then, in 2017, the Air Line Pilots Association reviewed irregularities in United’s seniority list. The union recommended removing Bumpus. United agreed, concluding that his recall rights had expired in 2012.

In January 2019, Bumpus sought to return and obtain medical leave to preserve his employment while resolving his medical certification. United initially told him his recall rights ran until March 2019. Days later, the airline reversed itself: its review with the union showed those rights had already expired.

He finally obtained a first class medical certificate in June 2020, nearly fourteen years after the stroke. United had offered to consider him as a new hire, but he didn’t apply. He wanted his original seniority.

Bumpus pursued a grievance and, in 2021, sued United and the union to obtain access to arbitration. The union wouldn’t take his case forward. He eventually got an arbitration hearing, but his grievance was dismissed as untimely in March 2023.

He filed a lawsuit in June 2023, seeking reinstatement with full seniority, lost pay and other damages. He alleged that United accommodated other pilots and brought back 111 pilots without military service while refusing to restore him. His claims under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act took two different approaches:

I’ve covered an American Airlines case involving a reservist who couldn’t legally fly but was nevertheless entitled to prompt reemployment in an appropriate role.

But Bumpus lost his reemployment claims in May 2025. The judge found that his absence from September 2001 to his accepted recall in May 2007 exceeded the law’s five-year service limit. He argued that time spent on economic furlough shouldn’t count: United wasn’t offering him work during those years anyway.

What remained was discrimination. Bumpus needed evidence that his military service was at least one reason for United’s actions. His argument about leave ran into a basic problem: he hadn’t requested it in 2007. He also hadn’t shown that the other pilots received leave without asking. United’s treatment of those pilots didn’t establish that it denied him the same benefit because he served in the military.

He did seek medical accommodation in 2019. By then, however, United and the union believed his recall rights had expired. The judge assumed, for purposes of deciding the case, that Bumpus was right about the 2019 deadline. Even with that assumption, he hadn’t shown military bias. United also removed two pilots with no military background after concluding their recall rights had expired, too. So even if United miscalculated, it wasn’t motivated by anti-military bias.

The pilot here wasn’t punished for his service. He couldn’t fly for United for years and they held out a spot for him anyway. It’s a complicated case that generated contradictory answers about exactly what his rights were under a union contract and government requirements. The union agreed he should lose his seniority. His medical clearance eventually expired again in 2024. He last flew for United a quarter century ago, and he can’t currently fly even if he wanted to.

Who’s ready for first class on United Airlines’s smallest regional jet?

The first Mitsubishi CRJ-450, a premium variant of the CRJ-200, is “on track” to begin carrying passengers by the end of the year. That's according to Andrew Nocella, United's chief commercial officer, who discussed the arrival of the CRJ-450 on the sidelines of the  brand-new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Monday.

The plane will debut at the airline’s Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD) hub, he added.

First look: United unveils gorgeous new Washington Dulles concourse, massive lounge

“It’ll be very exciting and it’s really critical that we connect big cities to little cities, and that’s what the CRJ-450 allows us to do,” said Nocella.

Nocella did not say where the CRJ-450 could fly from ORD but it is widely expected to serve some of the smallest cities in United's network, for example Akron-Canton, Ohio, or Fort Wayne, Indiana.

United unveiled the CRJ-450 in March in an effort to expand its premium offerings to smaller markets. Instead of the usual 50 economy seats on the CRJ-200, the 450 has seven first-class, 16 extra-legroom economy and 18 economy seats — for a total of 41 — a luggage closet for carry ons and high-speed Starlink inflight WiFi.

United's new CRJ-450: Could this be the fanciest regional jet in America?

The CRJ-450 is essentially a premium overhaul to the standard CRJ-200 that has been a workhorse of regional flying for much of this centutry. Passengers have routinely disliked the CRJ-200 for being small and cramped, an experience United hopes to improve with the less-dense CRJ-450 variant.

The plane is similar to the CRJ-550, a 50-seat premium variant of the CRJ-700 that typcially seats around 70 passengers. United debuted the CRJ-550 in 2019.

The CRJ-450 is the smallest plane in United’s premium airplane menu. Larger offerings include the Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” for premium domestic routes, the A321XLR for long-haul routes and up to the Boeing 787-9s with the “elevated” interior that features the new Polaris Studio in business class.

“We have realized that the demand for premium was much higher than we ever knew,” United CEO Scott Kirby, said in March. “It’s like we’re finally creating supply to meet the demand for premium.”

United regional affiliate SkyWest Airlines will operate the first 40 CRJ-450s under the United Express brand. The first two CRJ-200s are undergoing the necessary modifications and certification at one of the Utah-based regional carrier’s maintenance facilities, SkyWest President Wade Steel said at the end of October.

“The first airplanes just take longer naturally just because you’re working through the first-time issues,” he explained. Subsequent CRJ-200 conversions will take 2 to 3 weeks.

Steel, and SkyWest CEO Chip Childs, emphasized that the first CRJ-450s would enter service with United by the end of the year despite at the time having only about eight weeks left in 2026.

Both executives were bullish on the opportunity for the CRJ-450. Steel estimated demand for around 100 aircraft in the coming years as major airlines seek to increase premium offerings across their fleets.

“Putting first class seats on a CRJ-200 in a very good LOPA [Layout of Passenger Accommodation] with an outstanding interior is a very valuable aircraft,” said Steel

Delta Air Lines, for example, joined United in offering the CRJ-550 on regional routes in 2024. SkyWest flies the CRJ-550 for Delta.

American Airlines is the only major U.S. carrier not offering the CRJ-550. However, the airline can fly more larger regional jets, particularly the Embraer E175, than either Delta or United under a more lenient contract with its pilots.

#6148. American First Class Will Get Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights (700-899 Miles)

American Airlines will reportedly be making a very nice change to first class service on some short haul flights that didn’t previously qualify for a meal service, and it’s something I’m sure passengers will be happy to see.

As things currently stand, American serves meals in first class on flights of at least 900 miles during meal times (900 miles roughly correlates to a little over two hours of flying, on average).

In the US, this is basically the industry standard, as Delta and United have the same cutoff of 900 miles for serving meals. On flights shorter than that, airlines only offer drinks and a snack basket in first class.

It looks like American will soon be leading the industry when it comes to service in first class on shorter flights, as it brings back a program it used to offer.

JonNYC reports that American will soon be bringing back the “light bites” concept on flights of 700 to 899 miles (700 miles correlates to a little over 90 minutes of flying, on average). The exact timeline for this remains to be seen, but it sounds like this will debut on flights between New York and Chicago, which isn’t surprising.

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

It must be a decade at this point since American offered this concept. The idea was to serve mixed nuts on these flights in a ramekin, and then to offer some sort of fresh item that’s plated, and comes with cutlery, a napkin, etc. For example, I remember options including a small fruit & cheese plate, a hummus & veggie plate, etc.

It wasn’t really a full meal replacement, but it was better than the snack basket, and definitely showed some effort than just packaged snacks. It remains to be seen what exactly this iteration of the concept looks like, so I’ll report back when we learn more.

It goes without saying that expectations of premium cabin travelers differ massively around the globe. In the Middle East, it’s common to have a 30-minute business class flight with a lie flat bed, cappuccinos, champagne, and a substantial, tasty snack.

In Europe, you’re typically stuck with a pretty underwhelming hard product on short haul flights (just economy with a blocked middle), but regardless of the length of the flight, you’re almost always served something fresh, even if the flight time is well under an hour.

In the United States, we have the benefit of actually having a dedicated first class cabin with larger seats, but the soft product just isn’t great. You can be on a flight of nearly two hours and just be served packaged snacks.

We do have to give credit to Alaska for this, as it’s the only US carrier to serve some sort of fresh food on flights of under 900 miles. On most Alaska flights you’ll get a snack on shorter services, so kudos to the airline for that.

American Airlines is expected to once again serve fresh food in first class on flights of 700-899 miles. The exact timeline remains to be seen, but this marks a resumption of the mini-meals we saw the airline serve in first class many years back.

Among the “big three” US carriers, American will be the only one to serve fresh food in first class on flights of under 900 miles, so kudos to the airline for that. I’m curious to learn more details.

What do you make of American serving mini-meals on shorter first class flights?

#6147. Airport Lounges Are Packed—Travelers Demand $5,000 Annual Credit Card Fees To Keep The Masses Out

Airport lounges are so crowded that travelers are demanding $200 admission prices and $5,000 annual credit card fees to keep the “untouchables” out, arguing that the “true lounge caste” has been driven into the concourse while everyone else crowds around the buffet. There are also lounges where the line outside and the crowd inside make the benefit nearly worthless. Paying for somewhere comfortable to sit, and then being unable to find a seat, has become a really legitimate complaint – even if it’s mixed with real snobbery because it’s the ‘other’ people who shouldn’t be in there. “Premium” travel experience before 10am on a Sunday https://t.co/13PniAuksG — David Slotnick (@David_Slotnick) November 8, 2026 Status anxiety places airline lounges belong alongside BMWs, remote work, and ski trips as things that have lost their cachet as access spread. They’re still aspirational to the people getting in, while the people already inside are unhappy that increased access has lowered their relative status. View wyatt.today’s post on Twitter The original poster’s follow-up invokes the tens of thousands of his employer’s dollars he spends on flights, then uses a racial slur for other guests. It’s no longer about finding empty space inside. But most people just want a chance to use the benefit they’re paying for and maybe a snack without standing in line in the terminal like a schmuck to get an $895 ‘free’ drink. Wanting Quiet Space Isn’t Elitist One reply argues that a lounge defeats its purpose when it gets too crowded. It may still have food, a shower, or an airline agent to help when your flight gets delayed or cancels. But the core value proposition is escape from the terminal. I often just want a place to open my laptop without balancing it on my knees. And then having frictionless access to a snack, and the ability to run into the washroom without bringing all my stuff with me, are cherries on top. Nobel laureate James Buchanan’s theory of clubs explains this well. Sharing a facility spreads its costs across more people. Eventually, adding people creates enough congestion to make the experience worse. The membership and the size of the facility have to be considered together. There need to be access limits to preserve the value proposition of the facility. But since most people don’t use the space most of the time, it’s perceived option value that they’re purchasing and it continues to drive premium credit card acquisition and adoption. Lounges Got Better, And People Started Using Them Differently I’ve written about the claim that airport lounge culture represents American decline. The nostaglic view is just wrong. I remember ginger ale and Goldfish crackers, a photocopier in the Admirals Club, and packaged Tillamook cheese in United’s Red Carpet Clubs. Today’s better lounges offer actual meals and craft cocktails. When I visited Chase’s new Dallas–Fort Worth lounge, I found the best food inside a bank lounge that isn’t a Capital One Landing. Plus they have whiskey tastings, and facial treatments. The space is 18,000 square feet. These spaces are no longer just a room with seating, snacks and a fax machine. The same improvements help explain why lounges fill up. People go for the food People who might have stopped in to check e-mail now plan to eat a meal. They come more often and stay longer. A better lounge becomes a destination in its own right. The travel mix has changed. Traditional managed business travel is a smaller part of the story. Premium leisure travelers, families, and people combining work with a trip use the same spaces. A Monday – Thursday consultant arriving just before boarding and a family building in a generous airport buffer spend very different amounts of time. Credit cards have expanded access. That brings in more people, including travelers who wouldn’t buy a separate airline club membership. Uncertain security waits get people to the airport earlier. If security might take ten minutes or an hour, you allow for the hour. When it takes ten minutes, you’ve suddenly got time to spend. Even without an increase in the average security wait, greater uncertainty can mean more time in the airport. I laid out these problems for Delta years ago. Their more substantial food draws people in and keeps them there. And Delta doesn’t just admit customers with its own premium card – American Express Platinum cardmembers flying Delta can enter, too. Platinum’s standard allotment is now 10 visits and Delta Reserve’s is 15, with a spending route to unlimited access. Delta also limits entry before an originating flight to three hours prior to scheduled departure, with an exception for connections. A three-hour entry window still leaves plenty of time for a long visit. And if everyone arrives before the same bank of departures, an empty room earlier in the day doesn’t help. The number of people holding an eligible card isn’t the only number that matters. Double the average length of a visit, with the same flow of arrivals, and you double the average number of people occupying the lounge. I recently catalogued 70 new and expanded lounge projects. More space helps, but a new lounge also attracts people who previously skipped the experience. I’d underscore that which lounges we’re talking about matters a great deal. Spending $895 for a Platinum Card doesn’t on its own signal discernment, although I their Salt Lake lounge is quite nice. Capital One’s Landings at Washington National and LaGuardia offer genuinely good food and reservations. You enter and are shown to a table. That’s a totally different experience. You Could Buy Your Way Into Lounges In The 1960s, Too One commenter remembers the 1990s as a time when people earned their way in by flying. But American Airlines started selling lounge memberships in 1967, at $25 a year or $250 for life. Before that, their sales department handed out memberships. Paid lounge access was a function of the civil rights era – a nondiscriminatory way to determine who could enter. The claim that credit card lounges are bad while airline lounges are good doesn’t make sense. I’d happily choose a good Chase or Capital One lounge over plenty of airline clubs. And finding quiet lounges overseas doesn’t mean most overseas lounges are quiet. Have you ever tried to enter a Priority Pass lounge at Heathrow? Comfort Can Spread Even When Status Can’t The discussion of aspiration is revealing. Some people feel that accessibility is the inverse of aspiration – that’s true if what you’re aspiring to is being above other people. But you can also just aspire to a more comfortable trip, get it, and be pleased that other people can get it too. A product can also become less distinctive to its old customers while becoming an attainable aspiration for new ones. The people entering and the people complaining aren’t necessarily the same people. That’s why the comparison to remote work is revealing – someone getting to work from home doesn’t take away the time you save on your commute working from home. Treating it as a status symbol entails a tradeoff (‘when everyone has status, nobody does’). I’m glad more people can have a better trip. I also want the benefit I’ve paid for to be usable. I don’t usually bother with Centurion lounges, they aren’t as nice as Capital One and Chase lounges in many airports and there are too many people waiting to get in. When there’s a choice, I’ll pick elsewhere. But some of those Chase (Las Vegas! Phoenix!) and Capital One lounges (Denver!) can make the wait not worth the squeeze, too. Banks are selling more access than they can deliver. Sometimes I’ll just take the restaurant in the terminal. Of course most banks stopped paying for Priority Passs swipes at restaurants – which would be fair enough if they could accommodate travelers in their own lounges. Of course most banks stopped paying for Priority Passs swipes at restaurants – which would be fair enough if they could accommodate travelers in their own lounges. Topics on this pageAirport loungeCredit cardAmerican AirlinesAmerican ExpressBMWCapital OneChaseChase BankDavid SlotnickDelta Air LinesDenverHeathrow AirportLaGuardia AirportLas VegasPriority PassTillamookUnited Airlines+15 more More From View from the Wing

One commenter remembers the 1990s as a time when people earned their way in by flying. But American Airlines started selling lounge memberships in 1967, at $25 a year or $250 for life. Before that, their sales department handed out memberships. Paid lounge access was a function of the civil rights era – a nondiscriminatory way to determine who could enter.

The claim that credit card lounges are bad while airline lounges are good doesn’t make sense. I’d happily choose a good Chase or Capital One lounge over plenty of airline clubs. And finding quiet lounges overseas doesn’t mean most overseas lounges are quiet. Have you ever tried to enter a Priority Pass lounge at Heathrow?

The discussion of aspiration is revealing. Some people feel that accessibility is the inverse of aspiration – that’s true if what you’re aspiring to is being above other people. But you can also just aspire to a more comfortable trip, get it, and be pleased that other people can get it too. A product can also become less distinctive to its old customers while becoming an attainable aspiration for new ones. The people entering and the people complaining aren’t necessarily the same people. That’s why the comparison to remote work is revealing – someone getting to work from home doesn’t take away the time you save on your commute working from home. Treating it as a status symbol entails a tradeoff (‘when everyone has status, nobody does’). I’m glad more people can have a better trip. I also want the benefit I’ve paid for to be usable. I don’t usually bother with Centurion lounges, they aren’t as nice as Capital One and Chase lounges in many airports and there are too many people waiting to get in. When there’s a choice, I’ll pick elsewhere. But some of those Chase (Las Vegas! Phoenix!) and Capital One lounges (Denver!) can make the wait not worth the squeeze, too. Banks are selling more access than they can deliver. Sometimes I’ll just take the restaurant in the terminal. Of course most banks stopped paying for Priority Passs swipes at restaurants – which would be fair enough if they could accommodate travelers in their own lounges. The folks with lounge access through their employer are the problem! I pay the annual fee for my Chase Sapphire Reserve card and have never seen a line at a Chase lounge in Philly or Boston but have seen the Centurion lounge lines. Why? Most of those folks are using a business AmEx card paid for by their employer. If they had to pay that annual fee, I suspect there’d be no lines. That comment about a $5,000 annual fee is probably from someone whose employer pays it!

With EU261 in place in the U.S., lounges would rightfully accept everyone, at any time.

Good one, Matt. Anyway, I think Gary is right in his thinking. The lounges have gotten much better in their quality over the years. But travel has changed, and I think the crowding issue is a function of those changes, fueled by Americans becoming much wealthier with more to spend on travel, while at the same time, post-COVID, travel habits have leaned towards arriving earlier at the airport and having longer connections.

I meant to add that the lines at Delta Sky Club can be skipped if you are in F on DL. There is often some good lounge that you can go to that is crowded but not overcrowded, so long as you are in long-haul J (Polaris, DL One, Virgin) – except at LHR T5.

Another thing to consider is the cost of eating a meal at the airport for family versus getting a card with lounge or priority club access and having a free meal before the flight.

“Travelers” demand $5K credit card fees? Really? TRAVELERS?

And who is this source that speaks for all travelers? Is there a union for travelers that I should have joined that is speaking for me? Was there a massive survey of travelers that collected this data.

Or by “travelers” we don’t actually mean travelers — we mean one, maybe a couple, social media “influencers”.

Last 12 months: 5 RT to Europe on AA Flagship Biz at $5-$10K per trip. That’s 10 visits to Terminal D DFW Flagship Lounge. (Yes Gary, I agree the food is getting marginally better and I have yet to place order or eat in private dining.) Space is only getting worse.

I don’t get the whole lounge thing. Get to your departure gate 30 minutes before departure and be on your way. Should you arrive early find a quiet gate and open your laptop.

@Matt — I wish. EU261 provides excellent basic consumer protections, not “VIP” lounge membership. For a “premium” airport lounge experience, please consider the Delta One lounge (now at JFK, LAX, BOS, SEA, but not ATL, because those suckers at HQ are fortress hub hostages…)

And the occupancy rates on the private suites at the CSR LGA lounge are….?

I believe the biggest problem is the airlines haven’t added enough lounge space to keep up with increased premium cabin demand. Airlines could help by adding restrictions on who has access to lounges until they have constructed adequate space.

Enforce a jacket and tie dress code. You’ll instantly remove 95%+ of people.

Lounges have become entirely too desirable, what with halfway decent food and liquor I remember the JKF Sky Club offering Chex Mix with jug wine and a cheap Scotch universally rated as one of the worst whiskies ever bottled. The place was quiet and empty.

Well played Matt – Add that to the irony of the left, they are usually the most classist people when it comes to put their own skin in the game. It’s always the other ppl pocket they want to grab and unfortunately that’s why there so many of these parasites in politics.

Amateurs call for more-exclusive airport lounges. Professionals call for more-exclusive airports.

Haven’t had the pleasure of trying them myself, but those José Andrés tapas in the C1 lounges always look gorgeous!

“Status anxiety places airline lounges belong alongside BMWs, remote work, and ski trips as things that have lost their cachet as access spread. ”

The same with “elite” status in loyalty programs. So many more people with status despite dwindling returns. I keep thinking people will eventually wake up. But then when I see those long lines outside of lounges I realize humanity is doomed.

when we flew to UK in August the sfo AA lounge was absolutely ghetto – actually witnessed 2 women fighting – food & trash all over the floor – children eating buffet food w/ their fingers & spitting some back into the bowls –

If this is true….. those Elitists can fly private and not worry about the slaves beneath them!

“Sharing a facility spreads its costs across more people.”

“Eventually, adding people creates enough congestion to make the experience worse.”

And…”Nobody goes there anymore. It’s too crowded.” Yogi

A thought just struck me. I thought we go to the airport to fly a plane to a destination, for work or pleasure. The planes I fly offer decent food and drink.

Frankly, this obsession with lounges/clubs, to me, is just pretentious.

The solution would be for companies to retain the benefits of employees flying. And certainly not paying for any cc, except basic ones.

For all those that want better clubs for me, not thee, fly private.

Oh, and by the way, Gary, isn’t you who writes two or three times a year, there is no reason to waste your time by showing up at the airport early. As you say, you are wasting productive time.

Lounge demand is also a function of the degraded onboard experience in coach and even first class. You know you’re going to suffer on the plane so grabbing a drink and some food before flying is more important than it was 20 years ago. That’s another, possibly equal, core value proposition.

Nothing says “living the dream” quite like intentionally extending your stay at an airport so you can sit in a room that is marginally less depressing than the rest of the airport.

I have access to three different lounge programs and have used them approximately once. This is because my airport philosophy is simple: airports are not destinations. They are obstacles. The objective is to spend as little time there as possible.

The only time you’ll find me lingering at an airport is when an airline has involuntarily altered my schedule. At that point, I’ll grab a table at a decent restaurant and order exactly what I want instead of fighting over the last mini quiche and a warm can of Diet Coke.

If you’re flying enough to earn lounge status, or you’re already sitting up front and getting lounge access included, I genuinely don’t understand the excitement over free snacks. The math simply isn’t computing.

Then again, I also walk right past Starbucks every day. So perhaps I just lack the refined appreciation for overpaying for things I don’t actually need while convincing myself it’s an elite experience.

Haha, @john is on to something. I remember when upscale restaurants required at minimum a sports coat. A dress code for airport lounges that prohibit pajamas, shorts, t-shirts and flip-flops would definitely be less crowded. Of course the lounge would have to hire bouncers, perhaps from a strip club close to the airport like on Century Blvd.

It Is outrageous to have to wait in line for a lounge which you have paid to be able to use, especially when so many restrictions have been put in place to limit overcrowding.

It’s also annoying that food is one of the main benefits yet some lounge operators do nothing to provide food for those with certain dietary reservations.

I don’t think that charging 15000 is the answer to overcrowding. Limiting memberships is.

When it comes to booze the lounges have gotton worse. I remember getting Glen Morangie scotch in the Presidents club, Glenlivit 12 year scotch in the America West Club and Johnny Walker Black in the Crown room all for free and some were self pour. Now you get bottom shelf and pay a premium for the good stuff

I fully agree that lounge access should come at a MUCH higher costs to thin the herds, however I feel fairly certain that the beancounters at Amex (in particular) have run the numbers and determined that they have the best supply/demand equilibrium to maximize their profitability. I no longer attempt to use the Centurion lounges anymore; either I’m in the airline’s lounge if uncrowded, or whatever the best bar or eatery option is in the terminal. It’s a whole lot less stressful and more enjoyable. I should really get rid of my Platinum, but I’m far too hooked on the Fine Hotels and Membership Rewards points.

(1) Advance Waitlist (as Amex does) so you can minimize wait time at the airport

(2) Charge a per visit fee (not per person) – this would weed out the people who are just there because it is free

1 is the best but 3 is also good because it benefits families and relegates road warriors to the airline lounges where they belong.

How about these card issuers invest in their lounge network in proportion to the cards they have issued. Each person in that line has paid $895 to stand in that line.

Of course, why people do that is a mystery. But so are the drug addicts.

Many moons ago, lounge membership wasn’t tied to credit cards at all. It was paid membership only. The people at the front desk area were reservation agents, who had almost as much control in ticketing as the people at the gates. If something went bad with a flight, you headed to the lounge. Food was not as plentiful in the lounges.

I’m not sure the credit card lounge affiliation is sustainable. People go for the food, largely aren’t business travelers, and frankly in many cases the overpriced establishments have more elbow room than the lounges.

Everybody wants lounges to be more discerning and exclusive as long as they personally make the cut to get into those lounges. Then they can ignore the poors.

Good point on families, Wilson. At a hub like DFW or ATL breakfast for four in the terminal can run $80 or more, so lounge access pays for itself fast if you actually use it. Timing helps a lot, Sunday mornings and the late afternoon banks are the worst, midday is usually calmer. FWIW a free app like TripIt pushes gate changes and delays to your phone, so you can stay put until it’s really time to move. Pack snacks anyway for the inevitable full lounge day

@Thing 1, you nailed it. Evidently one jerk posted something on X (there’s a link). That doesn’t make “travelers,.”

#6146. Amex Business Gold Card Bonus: As High As 200K Points Welcome Offer

The American Express® Business Gold Card is one of the most rewarding business cards if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing an excellent Amex Business Gold Card welcome offer, which is the biggest bonus we’ve ever seen on the card, making it the ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Business Gold Card

The Amex Business Gold Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 200,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $15,000 on eligible purchases within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Find out your offer.

Amex uses a variety of factors when it comes to deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Gold Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible offer through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there. That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method.

It goes without saying that the Amex Business Gold bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to $5,000 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, 200,000 points are worth $3,400, which is an incredible offer, assuming you’re eligible. This is the biggest publicly available bonus that we’ve seen on this card, and in the past, we’ve often only seen offers of 70,000 to 100,000 points, so this is much better. I’d consider the Amex Business Gold Card bonus to be among the best welcome offers out there.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air France-KLM Flying Blue, to Emirates Skywards, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give a couple of examples of Amex points redemption opportunities:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Business Gold Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note when it comes to apply for Amex business cards:

Anecdotally, I find this to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Gold, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Gold Card has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees). There are many reasons to consider picking up this card.

I’d say the single biggest reason to get the Amex Business Gold is because of the rewards structure. Each billing cycle, the card earns 4x points in the two categories in which your business spends the most. There are a total of six eligible categories to choose from. Note that you earn 4x points on the first $150,000 in combined purchases from these categories each calendar year, and then 1x points thereafter.

Categories eligible for 4x points on the Amex Business Gold include the following:

The Amex Business Gold also offers 3x points per dollar spent on flights and prepaid hotels booked through Amex Travel (either on amextravel.com or the Amex Travel app), and 1x points on all other eligible purchases, with no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees).

On top of that, the Amex Business Gold offers up to $845 in annual credits, potentially more than offsetting the annual fee. The Amex Business Gold credits include the following:

Read a full review of the Amex Business Gold Card here.

There’s currently an excellent Amex Business Gold Card bonus, as the welcome offer is as high as 200,000 Membership Rewards points upon completing minimum spending. While the spending requirement is significant, so is the number of points you can earn, so this is worth it if you can swing it… assuming you’re eligible!

The main reason to consider picking up this card (beyond the great welcome offer) is because it offers 4x points in valuable categories. On top of that, though, the card offers some credits that can help offset the annual fee.

Do you plan on picking up the Amex Business Gold Card? What kind of a welcome offer are you eligible for?

#6145. Premium Travel Cards Now Cost Up To $895 But $95 Cards Still Deliver Outsized Rewards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

There’s no card that earns more for ongoing spending than the Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees). It’s a $495 annual fee card, and that I think that easily makes sense if you’re spending $25,000 or more a year on the card (that’s just a little over $2,000 a month).

But not everyone is going to invest in an expensive card. I talk most about products like this, and the $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees).

I think it’s really worth looking at mid-tier cards, also. Something more expensive than the no annual fee products, where you can still do quite well, but if you’re willing to invest a little but you can get outsized return.

I love Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (See rates and fees) for lounge access, and I think it’s easily worth the $395 annual fee considering it’s effectively rebated in value by the $300 annual credit for bookings through Capital One Travel and 10,000 bonus miles (equal to $100 towards travel) every year, starting on your first anniversary.

But if you don’t want to spend that much on an annual fee then Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (See rates and fees) still earns at least 2X miles on all purchases and they’re transferrable points. It has a $95 annual fee.

Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (See rates and fees) has an offer to earn 100k bonus points after you spend $8,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening.

What’s great is earning 3x (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases) on travel, shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, advertising purchases made with social media sites and search engines each account anniversary year.

It has the same points transfer partners as Chase Sapphire Reserve®, for a lot less money, and a lot of the points-earning for spend. And if you have some of the no annaul fee Chase cards, you can move the points from those cards over to Ink Business Preferred and then transfer them to airlines and hotel programs.

Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) This isn’t the ultra-premium Strate Elite. But you still earn 60,000 bonus ThankYou® Points after spending $4,000 in the first 3 months of account opening.

Where it shines is as a tool to earn for your spending at the $95 annual fee price point: Earn 10 Points per $1 spent on Hotels, Car Rentals, and Attractions booked on CitiTravel.com; Earn 3 Points per $1 on Air Travel and Other Hotel Purchases, at Restaurants, Supermarkets, Gas and EV Charging Stations; Earn 1 Point per $1 spent on all other purchases.

And points transfer to American Airlines AAdvantage, here’s the full list of partners:

Wells Fargo Autograph Journey is a sleeper because it’s a $95 annual fee card that earns 5x on hotels, 4x on airlines, and 3x on restaurants and other travel. That means it still bonuses Airbnb and cruises, which Sapphire Reserve does not. And they give you a $50 annual statement credit with a $50+ airline purchase each year, cutting the effective cost of that annual fee.

Where the card isn’t as strong is points transfers. They’ve promised more, but that’s happened very slowly. They transfer to the IAG Avios programs (Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia) as well as Air France KLM, Cathay Pacific, JetBlue, Virgin, Wyndham and Choice.

Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) is a $95 annual fee card that will earn up to 1.25X points on rent and mortgage payments with no transaction fee.

It’s great for card spending because it earns 3X on your choice of grocery (up to $25K/year) or dining. Your 3X category choice remains in effect for the entire calendar year. It also earns 2X points on travel. And it comes with a $100 Bilt Travel Hotel credit. Applied twice a year, as $50 statement credits, for qualifying Bilt Travel Portal hotel bookings.

The reason this is so strong is that, combined with points for rent or mortgage, you can be earning more than 4 points per dollar in your chosen category and these are the most valuable points and Bilt runs the biggest transfer bonuses. They partner with programs like Hyatt, United, Southwest, Alaska, and Japan Airlines. You don’t have to spend $395, $795 or $895 to earn valuable rewards. Which one of these works best for you depends on what your spend pattern looks like. Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card is probably best if you’re in a position to get a small business card. Wells Fargo Autograph Journey is great for heavy travel spend, if their transfer partners work for you. Citi Strata Premier® Card probably offers the best return for the way most people spend. While the Bilt Obsidian Card has the most potential upside if you play your hand well. #6144. America Needs an Arsenal of Democracies

We must combine American and allied innovation and manufacturing to take on the threats we share.

A worker along the assembly line handles large caliber 155mm metal projectiles at the Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Scranton, Pa., April 16, 2024.

An Israeli-developed missile is now rolling off an American production line. On October 9, Raytheon-Rafael Protection Systems, an American Israeli joint venture, announced the first Tamir interceptors manufactured in Camden, Ark. They are intended for Israel’s Iron Dome missile-defense system, with plans to produce a U.S. variant for the Marine Corps.

The Camden facility builds on decades of allied weapons production, including the AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile with West Germany as well as the F-16 with multiple partners. But today’s conflicts require an industrial network that produces weapons at scale, maintains deliveries during disruptions, and replenishes forces across theaters. Co-production alone does not deliver that. It changes where a weapon is built; resilience depends on whether production can continue when something breaks.

Mackenzie Eaglen is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, where she works on defense strategy, defense budgets, and military readiness.

Daniel Flesch is the Executive Director of the Defense Technology Alliance.

The Camden facility builds on decades of allied weapons production, including the AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile with West Germany as well as the F-16 with multiple partners. But today’s conflicts require an industrial network that produces weapons at scale, maintains deliveries during disruptions, and replenishes forces across theaters. Co-production alone does not deliver that. It changes where a weapon is built; resilience depends on whether production can continue when something breaks.

Mackenzie Eaglen is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, where she works on defense strategy, defense budgets, and military readiness.

Daniel Flesch is the Executive Director of the Defense Technology Alliance.

#6143. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

Bilt is changing how its credit cards earn rewards, and cardholders who want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash on everyday spending need to make a choice. New applicants must apply, be approved and accept their offer by December 31. I’ve already opted to keep the benefit—it’s a big reason my Bilt Palladium gets most of my spending.

Frequent Miler‘s latest ‘Ask Us Anything’ was a strong endorsement of Bilt. Their three Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) cardholders plan to renew, and even the group’s Bilt skeptic plans to apply. They all want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash.

If you don’t have a Bilt card, I’d get one now. You need to apply, get approved and accept the card offer by December 31, 2026 to preserve the choice of earning 4% Bilt Cash. Existing cardmembers also need to actively choose to keep it before their first card anniversary in 2027. Doing nothing means moving into the new rewards structure.

Nick Reyes calls renewing Palladium “pretty much a no-brainer.” It’s his “daily driver,” the card he uses most often. He’s happy earning two or three Bilt Points per dollar because they’re “very valuable,” with “plenty of great transfer partners” and continued good transfer bonuses. With a points accelerator active, he’ll often use it even for spending that another card would bonus. He’s approaching Platinum status (thanks to his card spend), but says the card’s earning makes sense even before transfer bonuses and status benefits.

Tim Steinke says he expects all three Palladium holders—Greg Davis-Kean, Nick and himself—to renew and retain the current rewards structure. Stephen plans to get the card before the old earning option closes, despite having no intended use for Bilt housing payments. He calls the points “absolutely fantastic.”

That’s also how I use the Bilt Palladium Card: it gets the majority of my spending. I pay my mortgage through Bilt, but the card would be valuable to me even without that.

I’ve written that Palladium looks complicated, but it’s the best everyday rewards card.

I consider these the most valuable points. You can redeem them at 1.25 cents apiece through Bilt’s travel portal, but I usually want to transfer them. The transfer partner lineup gives me access to:

Most transfers are 1:1. Accor is 3:2, I Prefer is 1:2, and Amtrak is 2:1. Bilt also runs large Rent Day transfer bonuses, often with better offers for higher elite tiers. I’ve used bonuses for transfers to Japan Airlines, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic and Air France KLM. Earning points quickly and then transferring with a bonus is why I want so much of my spending here.

Bilt is changing the earning choice in 2027. Today, cardmembers can choose:

Most cardmembers already choose the second option. Palladium is still a great card that way. But for most people putting significant spending on the card, especially when they’re generating more Bilt Cash than their housing payments would consume, I think the 4% option is better. Once you’ve reached the highest housing multiplier, spending more doesn’t increase that multiplier. With Flexible Bilt Cash, more spending keeps producing more Bilt Cash to use.

There are exceptions. I’ve explained how the housing option can produce an effective 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. At the 25% spending threshold, $1,000 of everyday spending and $4,000 of eligible housing payments earn 2,000 points from the purchases and 2,000 from housing. That’s 4,000 points against $1,000 of everyday spending. The relationship between your spending and housing payments determines which choice works best.

For me, the accelerators alone are a reason to preserve Bilt Cash earning. Spend $200 in Bilt Cash to activate one and you earn an extra point per dollar on the next $5,000 in eligible spending. Palladium’s 2X becomes 3X. That $5,000 also generates another $200 Bilt Cash, which can fund the next accelerator. Each eligible cardholder can activate five per calendar year.

My wife and I have both maxed out our accelerators this year: 3 points per dollar on $50,000 of combined spending. We’ve earned points on housing payments as well.

She has an authorized user card on my Palladium account. It costs $95 annually and comes with her own Priority Pass membership. She doesn’t receive a second set of my annual hotel and Bilt Cash credits, but she can earn rewards in her own Bilt account (or I can switch it to mine).

I’ve laid out how my wife and I use this. I directed the points and Bilt Cash from her spending into her account instead of mine. She earns her own status, funds her own accelerators, and can take advantage of transfer bonuses separately. When an offer bonuses transfers of up to 100,000 Bilt Points per member, two accounts give us room to bonus 200,000 points, with each person’s bonus determined by their own status.

An authorized user’s spending doesn’t automatically get the primary cardholder’s active accelerator. They need to activate their own, using their own Bilt Cash. Bilt also gives the primary cardholder separate card numbers and controls over authorized user spending, including transaction and monthly limits. You can add an authorized user starting at age 13. But for my wife and me, the separate rewards accounts are the reason this has been so useful.

And I’ve gotten far more out of Bilt Cash than just faster points earning. I’ve redeemed it for:

These are benefits I’ve actually used. For my everyday spending, Palladium earns the points I want faster than any other card, and the benefits have been incredible.

The new structure still allows Palladium and Obsidian cardmembers to use accelerators. Palladium’s $400 annual hotel credit and $200 annual Bilt Cash become a $600 annual Bilt Cash deposit at the card anniversary. That can fund three accelerators. Members can also earn Bilt Cash from other activity, including $50 for each 25,000 qualifying points. But they won’t replenish it at 4% of everyday spending.

Keeping the existing structure also preserves my separate $200 hotel credits, which I can stack with Bilt Cash hotel redemptions. The Bilt Cash hotel redemption allowance moves from monthly to twice yearly starting January 1 even for those keeping 4% earning, but I can still get the two $300 discounts this way.

Plus, Bilt Cash now expires at the end of the month 12 months after it’s earned. Cash earned in February 2026 lasts through February 28, 2027. The old rule would have wiped out everything over $100 at year-end. Having more time to use what I earn makes the 4% option better for me.

If you don’t have a card, I’d apply now and complete approval and acceptance before December 31. My choice is Bilt Palladium. The ability to preserve 4% Bilt Cash also applies to the Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) and no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (See rates and fees).

And if you already have a card, don’t assume your current selection of Flexible Bilt Cash protects you from the change. You need to proactively choose to keep it. I’ve already done this:

The new rewards model is selected by default. Swipe right.

You have until your first card anniversary in 2027 to make that election. Preserve it now and you can still move to the new structure later. Once that switch takes effect, you can’t move back. That’s why getting a Bilt Palladium Card makes so much sense – keeping the earning option. They’ll pry the 4% Bilt Cash earning option from my cold, dead hands, as they say.

#6140. Why Russia Is Targeting European Freezers

Rearmament isn’t just for the battlefield — civil defense matters, too.

A woman walks past partially empty shelves at a SuperValu store in Blanchardstown, Dublin, Ireland, November 2, 2026.

Twice in the space of a few weeks, Russian hackers have managed to seize control of supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. It began with hundreds of French stores in mid-October, after which, in early November, hackers struck outlets in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, and elsewhere. The hackers remotely forced freezers and chillers into prolonged defrost mode, driving temperatures to more than 120 degrees Fahrenheit and spoiling large quantities of food. These attacks have revealed an underrated aspect of rearmament that has so far been almost completely overlooked: civil defense.

Hackers behind most ransomware attacks demand payment. These hackers simply disrupted Europe’s food supply and left without a message. Only a few days after the most recent (as of this writing) attacks, in early November, did a Russian group finally claim responsibility. European policymakers who may have wished that some random teenagers were behind the attacks instead had their fears confirmed: This was a Russian attack against Europe’s food supply.
